It gives huge freedom—but there’s a catch: many FMO models only limit stiffness size, not whether that stiffness could actually come from mixing two real materials (a soft phase and a stiff phase).

This paper tackles that “is it physically buildable?” question in 2D structures made from **two isotropic materials**. The authors build a **three-level hierarchy of realism checks** based on classic energy bounds: a loose “zeroth-order” box, a tighter **Voigt** bound, and the tightest **Hashin–Shtrikman (HS)** bound. As the bounds tighten, the best possible compliance (flexibility under load) gets worse—but more realistic.

They prove key math results (solutions exist; sets nest strictly except at pure-material limits) and show Voigt reduces to a simple “variable thickness sheet” model. HS is harder (nonconvex), so they solve an **orthotropic** HS version using **sequential global programming**, and validate it on cantilever and multi-load problems. HS predictions closely match laminate-based reference designs for single loads, while for multiple loads HS gives a reliable lower bound.

title: Coupling of the continuum and semiclassical limit. Part I: convergence of eigenvalues
abstract: We analyze the semiclassical $d$-dimensional Schrödinger operator in the continuum $ \frac{1}{2} \Delta + \lambda_N^2 V$ discretized on a mesh with spacing proportional to $1/N$. The semi-classical parameter $\lambda_N$ is chosen as $\lambda_N = N^{1 - \gamma}$, with $\gamma \in (-1,1)$, which ensures that $N$ governs both the semiclassical and continuum limit simultaneously. We prove that all eigenvalues of the discrete operator converge to those of the continuum, as $\lambda_N\to\infty$. Beyond this semi-classical domain, in the case of the harmonic oscillator, we further discuss the spectral asymptotics for $\gamma \in \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1,1)$, thereby fully characterizing the eigenvalue behavior across all possible values of $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$.
gpt_response:
Imagine modeling an electron moving through a crystal. In the real world, space is continuous, but in a computer—or in a lattice model—space becomes a grid of points. This paper studies what happens to the *energy levels* (eigenvalues) of a “discrete Schrödinger operator” on a \(d\)-dimensional grid as the grid gets finer.

The key twist is that the authors don’t refine the grid and take the “classical limit” separately. Instead, they tie both together using one scaling knob, called \(\gamma\). By varying \(\gamma\), they uncover **five distinct limiting behaviors**. In the most important window, \(\gamma\in(-1,1)\), they prove that *every* energy level—after the right rescaling—converges to the same values predicted by the usual continuous Schrödinger equation in the semiclassical regime.

To build the proof, they first solve the discrete harmonic oscillator case, using Hermite-polynomial-based “almost eigenfunctions,” plus localization tools (the IMS formula) to control errors. Then they extend the result to smooth, nonnegative potentials with finitely many well-shaped minima and positive growth at infinity. A companion paper will tackle how the corresponding wavefunctions behave.

title: Interface for variants of the contact process
abstract: We study two one-dimensional variants of the contact process: the contact-and-barrier process, where the population evolves in a region delimited by a randomly moving barrier, and the multitype contact process, in which two species compete for space. The contact-and-barrier process is started with the barrier at the origin and all sites to its right occupied, while the multitype contact process is started from the Heaviside configuration with species 1 to the left of the origin and species 2 to the right. We prove that both models exhibit tight interfaces and that, after centring by an appropriate deterministic speed, the interface position satisfies a central limit theorem. Our analysis relies on a renewal-time method based on a novel construction called patchwork construction, in which the processes are built by concatenating space-time evolutions over successive time intervals of random length, providing a more convenient framework for defining the renewal times that drive the proofs.
gpt_response:
Imagine a line of houses where an “infection” can spread. In the classic contact process, an infected house can recover, and healthy houses can catch the infection from infected neighbors. A key discovery from earlier work is a tipping point: below a certain spread strength, the infection almost surely dies out; above it, it can survive and its frontier moves at a steady average speed.

This paper explores two twists on that idea. First is the **contact-and-barrier** model: the infection lives only to the right of a single moving barrier. The barrier randomly steps left or right, and if it steps onto an infected site it can wipe it out. Starting from a sharp “all infected on the right” setup, the authors prove the barrier eventually travels with a well-defined constant speed. Even more, the narrow “battle zone” between barrier and infection stays bounded in size over time, and the interface position shows random wiggles that, after rescaling, follow the familiar bell-curve pattern.

Second is a **two-species** version where two infections compete and cannot invade each other’s occupied sites. When both species are strong enough to survive alone, the interface again stays tight and its position obeys a bell-curve fluctuation law.

The technical engine is a clever “patchwork” construction that chops time into renewal blocks with repeatable, independent behavior.

title: Stochastic Differential Inclusions driven by Maximal Monotone Operators with empty interiors
abstract: This paper studies the long-time behavior of stochastic differential inclusions driven by maximal monotone operators, motivated by continuous-time models of first-order optimization methods under noisy or approximate operator information. We first address well-posedness and show that existence and uniqueness can be established without the customary requirement that the operator's domain has nonempty interior, by adopting an appropriate notion of solution. We then analyze asymptotic properties of the resulting stochastic dynamics, extending convergence guarantees beyond previously studied settings that rely on smooth potentials, full-domain subdifferentials, or Lipschitz monotone operators. In addition, we consider a Tikhonov-type regularization of the stochastic inclusion and prove corresponding well-posedness and long-time convergence results.
gpt_response:
Imagine trying to roll a ball to the lowest point of a landscape, but your measurements of the slope are noisy. Mathematicians model this with a “flow” that moves downhill to minimize a convex function. This paper studies a much broader noisy version, where the “downhill direction” can be set-valued (there may be many valid directions), described by a general maximal monotone operator.

A key obstacle is that earlier theories usually assumed the allowed region has some “thickness” (nonempty interior). The authors remove this restriction by redefining what it means to be a solution: they add an extra random term that captures noise pushing the motion in directions that don’t affect the constrained region. With this new definition, they prove existence and uniqueness of solutions in full generality.

Then they analyze long-term behavior when the noise gradually weakens. They show the time-averaged position converges to a true solution, and if the noiseless system converges, the noisy one converges too—sometimes with explicit rates. For subgradient flows (nonsmooth convex optimization), they also bound how fast function values approach the minimum and give probability “concentration” guarantees.

Finally, adding a slowly vanishing “Tikhonov” pull toward the origin forces convergence to the minimum‑norm solution, improving stability and selection.

title: Gaussian fluctuations for hyperbolic Anderson model with Lévy colored noise
abstract: In this article, we study the asymptotic behaviour of the spatial integral $F_R(t)$ of the solution to the hyperbolic Anderson model in dimension $d=1$, driven by the Lévy colored noise introduced in Balan and Jiménez (2026). We assume that the spatial coloration kernel of the noise is either integrable on $\mathbb{R}$, or is the Riesz kernel of order $\alpha \in (0,1)$, and the Lévy measure of the noise has finite moments of order $p$ and $2p$ for some $p \in (1,2]$. By applying a recent result of Trauthwein (2025), we prove that $F_R(t)/\sqrt{{\rm Var}\big(F_R(t)\big)}$ converges to the standard normal distribution as $R \to \infty$, and we give an estimate for the rate of this convergence in the Fortet-Mourier distance, the 1-Wasserstein distance, or the Kolmogorov distance. We also provide the corresponding functional limit result.
gpt_response:
Many real-world systems—like turbulent air, rough surfaces growing, or waves moving through messy materials—are shaped by randomness. Mathematicians model these with **stochastic partial differential equations** (SPDEs). This paper studies a wave-type SPDE called the **hyperbolic Anderson model** in 1D, where the randomness comes from a **Lévy noise**: instead of gentle Gaussian “static,” it includes sudden jumps. The noise is also **colored**, meaning nearby points in space are correlated through a smoothing kernel.

The authors look at a big-window measurement: take the solution \(u(t,x)\), subtract its average value (here it’s 1), and **add it up over the interval \([-R,R]\)**. As \(R\) grows, they prove three key things. First, the field is **ergodic**, so large spatial averages settle down to zero. Second, they compute how the **variance scales** with \(R\), with two regimes depending on whether the kernel is integrable or a long-range “Riesz-type” kernel. Third, they prove a **quantitative central limit theorem**: after rescaling, the spatial sum becomes approximately Gaussian, and they give an explicit convergence rate. They also extend this to a **functional CLT**, showing the whole time-evolving curve converges to a Gaussian process. The main tools combine **Poisson–Malliavin calculus** (to control sensitivity to jumps) with modern normal-approximation techniques.

title: Structure Theorems for locally compact modules over localizations of the integers
abstract: Given a multiplicatively closed subset $S$ of the integers, there exist Structure Theorems for $LC$ modules over the localization $\mathbb{Z}S^{-1}$ that are "similar" to those of $LCA$ groups. The most notable one is the 1st Theorem: Given such a module $M$, there exists a unique set of prime numbers $\Sigma$ (purely dependent on $S$) for which $M \cong \mathbb{R}^n \times \sideset{}{'}\prod_{q \in \Sigma} \mathbb{Q}_p^{n_p} \times N$, where $(n, (n_p)_{p \in \Sigma})$ is a sequence of nonnegative integers and $N$ contains a compact open submodule $K$ such that $K/K_0$ is a topological module over $\prod_{ q \in \mathbb{P}\setminus{\Sigma}} \mathbb{Z}_q$. Just like for $LCA$ groups, it is also possible to characterize the locally compact, compactly generated modules over $\mathbb{Z}S^{-1}$, as well as their Pontryagin Duals (which then allows to conclude that any locally compact $\mathbb{Z}S^{-1}$-module is an inverse limit of modules within a specific family). These characterizations are given in the 2nd and 3rd Structure Theorems respectively. Furthermore, as an elementary consequence of the 1st Structure Theorem, one can obtain a full classification of locally compact vector spaces over $\mathbb{Q}$.
gpt_response:
Mathematicians often study “groups” that also carry a notion of distance and closeness—so you can talk about limits and continuity. This paper looks at such *locally compact* abelian groups that also allow “scaling” by numbers from a ring like \(\mathbb{Z}\) with some primes inverted (a localization). A key surprise: even if an abstract group can be scaled this way, the scaling might fail to be continuous, so the authors focus on cases where continuity holds.

To analyze these objects, the paper uses **Pontryagin duality**, a technique that replaces a group by the space of all continuous “frequency probes” (characters). With tools like annihilators (which record what those probes can’t detect), compact elements, and an adapted Open Mapping Theorem, the authors prove **structure theorems**: any compactly generated module splits into understandable building blocks—free parts, compact parts, and “adelic” parts.

A major contribution is introducing **adelic rings** tied to the chosen primes and showing that locally compact modules over the *finite adeles* decompose as restricted products of finite-dimensional \(p\)-adic vector spaces. The paper also classifies locally compact \(\mathbb{Q}\)-vector spaces and ends with open questions about which modules are “Lie type,” meaning they locally resemble powers of the adele ring.

title: Iteration Complexity of Frank-Wolfe and Its Variants for Bilevel Optimization
abstract: We study Frank-Wolfe (FW) methods for constrained bilevel optimization when the lower-level problem is solved only approximately, yielding biased and inexact hypergradients. We analyze inexact variants of vanilla FW as well as away-step and pairwise FW, and provide convergence rates in the nonconvex setting under gradient errors. By combining these results with recent bounds on hypergradient errors from iterative and approximate implicit differentiation, we derive overall iteration complexity guarantees for bilevel FW. Experiments on two real-world applications validate the theory and demonstrate practical effectiveness.
gpt_response:
Many machine-learning tasks are really “two problems stacked together.” At the lower level, you train a model (find good weights). At the upper level, you tune choices like hyperparameters or data weights so the trained model performs well on a validation set. The catch: the upper-level decision depends on the lower-level solution, which is often too expensive to compute exactly—so even the “direction to improve” (the gradient) is only approximate.

This paper studies how to optimize the upper level **without costly projection steps** onto complicated constraint sets. Instead, it uses **Frank–Wolfe** methods, which only need an easier subroutine: minimizing a linear function over the constraint set. The authors analyze three versions—vanilla Frank–Wolfe, an **away-step** variant, and a **pairwise** variant—when the gradient is biased because the lower problem is solved only approximately.

They combine these methods with two popular ways to estimate the needed “hypergradient”: **Iterative Differentiation** and **Approximate Implicit Differentiation**. The main contribution is a first set of theoretical guarantees showing these projection-free methods still converge, with a clear link between lower-level work and overall progress. Experiments on semi-supervised learning and data distillation show the variants typically beat vanilla Frank–Wolfe after an initial slow phase.

title: Accelerated Online Risk-Averse Policy Evaluation in POMDPs with Theoretical Guarantees and Novel CVaR Bounds
abstract: Risk-averse decision-making under uncertainty in partially observable domains is a central challenge in artificial intelligence and is essential for developing reliable autonomous agents. The formal framework for such problems is the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where risk sensitivity is introduced through a risk measure applied to the value function, with Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) being a particularly significant criterion. However, solving POMDPs is computationally intractable in general, and approximate methods rely on computationally expensive simulations of future agent trajectories. This work introduces a theoretical framework for accelerating CVaR value function evaluation in POMDPs with formal performance guarantees. We derive new bounds on the CVaR of a random variable X using an auxiliary random variable Y, under assumptions relating their cumulative distribution and density functions; these bounds yield interpretable concentration inequalities and converge as the distributional discrepancy vanishes. Building on this, we establish upper and lower bounds on the CVaR value function computable from a simplified belief-MDP, accommodating general simplifications of the transition dynamics. We develop estimators for these bounds within a particle-belief MDP framework with probabilistic guarantees, and employ them for acceleration via action elimination: actions whose bounds indicate suboptimality under the simplified model are safely discarded while ensuring consistency with the original POMDP. Empirical evaluation across multiple POMDP domains confirms that the bounds reliably separate safe from dangerous policies while achieving substantial computational speedups under the simplified model.
gpt_response:
Imagine a firefighting drone or a trading bot that must act fast even when it can’t fully “see” what’s going on. Researchers often model this kind of uncertainty with POMDPs—decision problems where the agent only has noisy clues about the true situation. The catch: solving POMDPs exactly is usually too slow.

This paper tackles a tougher version: **risk-averse** planning, where the agent cares most about the *worst-case slice* of outcomes, using a measure called **CVaR** (think: “average of the worst losses,” not just the average result). The authors propose speeding things up by planning with a **simplified model** that’s cheaper to simulate, but then adding math-based **upper and lower bounds** that guarantee how risky the *real* model could be.

Key idea: if the simplified model’s outcome distribution is close to the real one (they track this mismatch over time), you can safely estimate CVaR and even **eliminate actions** that are provably bad. Using particle-based simulations and offline/online estimation tricks, they show big speedups (up to ~20×) with almost no drop in performance across several benchmark tasks.

title: R-triviality for adjoint classical groups of type C
abstract: For a central simple algebra with a symplectic involution (A,s) over a field of characteristic different from 2, we show that its group of projective similitudes PSim(A,s) is R-trivial in two new cases.
gpt_response:
Some symmetry groups in algebra behave like smooth, connected landscapes: you can slide from one point to another along simple “paths.” Mathematicians call this property **R-triviality**. This paper investigates when a particular symmetry group—built from a highly structured number system (a *central simple algebra*) equipped with a “mirror-like” operation called a **symplectic involution**—has that connectedness.

Earlier work showed the group is well-behaved when its size parameter is odd, and also in the smallest even case. The authors tackle harder even cases using a key tool by Merkurjev, which translates the geometric question (“are all points connected by paths?”) into checking certain number-theoretic data called **multipliers** and **norms** after extending the field.

Their main results: for degree 8 algebras whose internal complexity (the *index*) is at most 2, the group is R-trivial. They also prove R-triviality for degree 12 when the index is at most 2 and a cohomological “discriminant” invariant vanishes. But they highlight known counterexamples at degree 8, index 4, and end with an open problem for degree 12, index 4.

title: Matroids from gain graphs over quotient groups
abstract:
We present a new construction for matroids from gain graphs that simultaneously generalizes several existing constructions. The construction takes as input a gain graph over a Frobenius group $\Gamma$ with Frobenius kernel $\Gamma_1$ and outputs an elementary lift of the frame matroid of the underlying gain graph over the quotient group $\Gamma/\Gamma_1$.
While the hypothesis that $\Gamma$ is a Frobenius group may seem unusual, we prove that it is in some sense necessary: if $\Gamma$ is any finite group with a nontrivial proper normal subgroup $\Gamma_1$ and there is a construction that takes in a complete $\Gamma$-gain graph and outputs an elementary lift $M$ of the frame matroid of the underlying $(\Gamma/\Gamma_1)$-gain graph so that a cycle of the graph is a circuit of $M$ if and only if it is $\Gamma$-balanced, then $\Gamma$ is a Frobenius group with Frobenius kernel $\Gamma_1$.
gpt_response:
Imagine a graph where every arrow on every edge carries a “move” from a group—like a rotation, a flip, or a shift. If you walk around a loop and the moves cancel out back to “do nothing,” that loop is called **balanced**. Decades ago, mathematician Thomas Zaslavsky showed how to turn such labeled graphs (“gain graphs”) into two different independence systems called **matroids**, known as the *frame* and *lift* matroids.

This paper builds a single, more flexible recipe that includes both of Zaslavsky’s constructions—and also newer ones used in geometry and rigidity (how structures stay stiff under symmetry). The authors assume the group contains a special normal subgroup, and that the remaining non-identity elements can be neatly split into subgroups with a strong “non-overlap under conjugation” property. Under these conditions, every gain graph produces a **canonical matroid** on its edges, and this matroid is always just one “step” away from a frame matroid built from the quotient group.

They also prove a partial converse: for large complete gain graphs over finite groups, any elementary-lift matroid that treats balanced cycles exactly as circuits must come from their construction—forcing the group to have Frobenius-group structure.

title: Local boundedness for weak solutions to fractional porous medium equation
abstract: We establish local boundedness for solutions to fractional porous medium-type equations in the fast diffusion regime, under optimal tail assumptions.
gpt_response:
Imagine a liquid seeping through a sponge—but with a twist: what happens at one point can be influenced by far-away points. That “long‑distance” effect is captured by a *fractional* porous‑medium equation, the focus of this paper. The authors study **weak solutions** (solutions that may be rough) and ask a basic but crucial question: **do solutions stay bounded, or can they blow up to infinity?**

Their key discovery is a **critical threshold** for the exponent \(q\), which controls how strongly the material diffuses. If \(q\) is **below or equal to the critical value**, then any nonnegative weak sub‑solution is automatically **locally bounded**—no extra assumptions needed. This matches what is known in the classical (non‑fractional) case.

To prove it, they combine two classic tools from PDE theory: an **energy estimate** (Caccioppoli-type) and a **step‑by‑step shrinking argument** (De Giorgi iteration). The hard part is the nonlocal operator, which brings in a “**tail**”: influence from outside the region. The authors introduce a **time‑dependent cutoff level** designed to cancel this tail, leading to the **first optimal boundedness results** for these fractional porous‑medium equations, plus **explicit bounds** when additional integrability is available in the supercritical regime.

title: Mekler's Construction and the Preservation of NCTP and NBTP
abstract: We give criteria for a first-order theory to be NCTP or NBTP using tree-indiscernibility. As an application, we show that Mekler's construction preserves NCTP and NBTP.
gpt_response:
Imagine you have any logical “world” you can describe with rules—like a network, a geometry, or a database. Mekler’s construction is a clever machine that turns that world into a special kind of algebraic object: a group built from a graph. Even though the original structure and the new group aren’t perfect mirrors of each other, this machine has a surprising talent: many deep “tameness” properties studied in modern logic survive the translation.

This paper focuses on two newer tameness tests, called NCTP and NBTP. They’re designed to capture when a theory avoids certain runaway patterns of consistency and contradiction arranged along branching tree shapes. The authors first give fresh, more usable ways to recognize NCTP and NBTP using highly symmetric “indiscernible” trees—trees where many parts look logically identical.

Then comes the main result: if the original theory is NCTP (or NBTP), the theory of its Mekler group is still NCTP (or NBTP). In short, Mekler’s construction preserves these two dividing lines too, extending a long list of properties already known to be preserved.

title: Frequency-Ordered Tokenization for Better Text Compression
abstract: We present frequency-ordered tokenization, a simple preprocessing technique that improves lossless text compression by exploiting the power-law frequency distribution of natural language tokens (Zipf's law). The method tokenizes text with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), reorders the vocabulary so that frequent tokens receive small integer identifiers, and encodes the result with variable-length integers before passing it to any standard compressor. On enwik8 (100 MB Wikipedia), this yields improvements of 7.08 percentage points (pp) for zlib, 1.69 pp for LZMA, and 0.76 pp for zstd (all including vocabulary overhead), outperforming the classical Word Replacing Transform. Gains are consistent at 1 GB scale (enwik9) and across Chinese and Arabic text. We further show that preprocessing accelerates compression for computationally expensive algorithms: the total wall-clock time including preprocessing is 3.1x faster than raw zstd-22 and 2.4x faster than raw LZMA, because the preprocessed input is substantially smaller. The method can be implemented in under 50 lines of code.
gpt_response:
When you zip a text file, the compressor is basically hunting for repeated byte patterns. The problem is that plain text spreads information across lots of different bytes, even though language itself is highly repetitive: a few common pieces (“the”, “ing”, punctuation) appear again and again. This paper proposes a simple “make-text-more-zip-friendly” preprocessing step.

First, it breaks text into **subword chunks** using the same Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization used in many AI language models. Unlike word-only tricks, subwords handle endings, rare words, Chinese, and Arabic without special rules. Next, it **relabels tokens by frequency**: the most common chunks get the smallest ID numbers. Finally, it writes those IDs using **variable-length integers**, so small IDs usually take just one byte.

On Wikipedia benchmarks (enwik8/enwik9), this boosts classic LZ-style compressors by **1–7 percentage points**, beating an older word-replacement method. Surprisingly, it can also make heavy compressors faster: for **zstd-22** and **LZMA**, total compression became **3.1×** and **2.4×** faster because the preprocessed stream is much smaller. It helps LZ compressors most, but can slightly hurt statistical ones like PPMd.

title: On a conjecture of Fujino and Sato
abstract: We revisit results of Fujino--Sato on complete non-projective $\mathbb Q$-factorial toric varieties and their conjectural factorization by flips. We show that their main results admit short conceptual proofs, avoiding any restriction on the dimension and the Picard number, from the general theory of Cox rings and Mori Dream Spaces, once one organizes small $\mathbb Q$-factorial modifications via the GKZ (secondary fan) decomposition of the moving cone. Moreover, we extend this viewpoint beyond the toric case by proving an analogous statement for complete $\mathbb Q$-factorial weak Mori Dream Spaces: any non-projective such variety admits a divisor $D$ and a $D$-flip to a (projective) Mori Dream Space. Our approach highlights the role of chambers and wall-crossing in the secondary fan as a unifying framework for these constructions.
gpt_response:
Imagine a complicated 3D map where each region tells you a different “version” of the same geometric world. This paper explains how to navigate that map for a class of shapes called **toric varieties**, which are built from combinatorial data and are popular testbeds in algebraic geometry.

Fujino and Sato had shown that **any complete toric variety can be birationally changed into a projective, well-behaved (ℚ-factorial) toric variety**, without altering anything in “most” dimensions (it stays the same outside lower-dimensional trouble spots). They also conjectured that you can always reach a projective model through a **finite chain of simple surgeries**—flips, flops, and anti-flips—proving it in a special 3D smooth case.

The note’s first contribution is to re-derive these results using the modern “Mori Dream Space” toolkit and the **secondary fan (GKZ) decomposition**: the movable cone is split into chambers, and **crossing a wall corresponds to performing a flip**.

Second, the author extends the idea beyond toric geometry: for any **non-projective weak Mori Dream Space**, there exists a divisor that triggers a flip leading to a **projective Mori Dream Space**. The key message: the chamber structure, not toric tricks, drives the whole story.

title: A note on varieties of ordered algebras
abstract: The aim of this work is to study the notions of lax protomodular and Ord-Mal'tsev category at the level of (coherent) varieties of (pre)ordered algebras and to further compare them, as has been done in the non-ordered context. We characterise varieties of ordered algebras which are (co)lax protomodular and those which are Ord-Mal'tsev, in terms of operations of arities given by ordered sets and inequalities involving them. We exhibit examples of (co)lax protomodular non-degenerate Ord-categories, which were unknown. We prove that, for varieties of ordered algebras which are Ord-Mal'tsev categories, the order of their algebras is degenerate (i.e. is symmetric). As a consequence, the implication "protomodular => Mal'tsev" cannot be carried out to our context. The case of non-coherent ordered varieties which are Ord-Mal'tsev categories is also addressed, where we show the existence of algebras with non-degenerate order.
gpt_response:
Category theorists like to study “families” of algebraic systems the way biologists study species. Two famous families, **protomodular** and **Mal’tsev** categories, generalize many useful facts about groups. This paper asks: what happens if our algebraic objects also carry an **order** (a “≤” relation), and all operations must respect it?

The authors replace the usual construction called a pullback with a more order-friendly gadget (a **comma object**). That creates two ways to “change viewpoint” along a map—called **vertical** and **horizontal**—leading to **lax** and **colax protomodularity**. Their main result characterizes exactly when a *pointed* ordered-algebra variety is lax or colax protomodular: it must have certain basic operations that let you “recover” an element from a comparison with another one, in a way compatible with the order. This yields concrete nontrivial examples, answering an open question about whether such ordered categories exist.

For the ordered version of the Mal’tsev property, they find a similar operation-based test—but surprisingly prove that in the coherent (order-respecting) setting it forces the order to collapse into symmetry (so “≤” behaves like equality). Finally, they show this collapse can fail in **non-coherent** ordered theories, giving an example where the Mal’tsev condition holds while the order remains genuinely one-way.

title: Existence of Quantum Splines via Fourth-Order Gradient Flows
abstract: We establish a rigorous existence theory for the quantum splines introduced by Brody, Holm, and Meier in Physical Review Letters (2012). These curves arise as solutions of a variational problem on the unitary group describing optimally controlled quantum evolutions. By formulating the problem within a geometric gradient flow framework for Riemannian spline interpolation, we construct a well-posed fourth order evolution whose asymptotic limits realize the desired quantum splines. The analysis requires adapting the variational structure to boundary conditions dictated by the physical model, which are not directly amenable to the setting in our recently developed framework for gradient flows of Riemannian spline interpolation. We show that, despite these difficulties, the modified system admits a rigorous analytical treatment, yielding both existence and a constructive procedure for generating quantum splines. Our results provide a mathematical foundation for the variational description of smooth quantum control trajectories and clarify the analytical structure underlying their formation.
gpt_response:
Imagine trying to steer a quantum system so that, at several scheduled moments, it lands on chosen “target” states—while keeping the control as smooth and gentle as possible. That’s the idea behind **quantum splines**: smooth paths of quantum evolution operators (the matrices that describe how a quantum state changes) that follow Schrödinger’s rule and minimize how violently the underlying control signal (the Hamiltonian) has to change. If the path misses the targets, a penalty term measures how far off it is.

Earlier work defined these splines but mainly offered numerical ideas and left a key issue: the boundary conditions at the final time were not enough to guarantee a well-defined evolution. This paper fixes that by adding natural end-point conditions and then proving an **existence theory**.

The authors build the spline by running a “smoothing” process called a **gradient flow**—like heat flow that gradually irons out wrinkles—based on a fourth-order geometric evolution equation. They prove short-time and long-time solutions using classical PDE tools, and show that as time goes on, the flow settles into a limit curve. That limit is a genuine quantum spline, closely related to a well-known geometric object: a Riemannian cubic on the space of unitary operations.

title: Learning Tangent Bundles and Characteristic Classes with Autoencoder Atlases
abstract: We introduce a theoretical framework that connects multi-chart autoencoders in manifold learning with the classical theory of vector bundles and characteristic classes. Rather than viewing autoencoders as producing a single global Euclidean embedding, we treat a collection of locally trained encoder-decoder pairs as a learned atlas on a manifold. We show that any reconstruction-consistent autoencoder atlas canonically defines transition maps satisfying the cocycle condition, and that linearising these transition maps yields a vector bundle coinciding with the tangent bundle when the latent dimension matches the intrinsic dimension of the manifold. This construction provides direct access to differential-topological invariants of the data. In particular, we show that the first Stiefel-Whitney class can be computed from the signs of the Jacobians of learned transition maps, yielding an algorithmic criterion for detecting orientability. We also show that non-trivial characteristic classes provide obstructions to single-chart representations, and that the minimum number of autoencoder charts is determined by the good cover structure of the manifold. Finally, we apply our methodology to low-dimensional orientable and non-orientable manifolds, as well as to a non-orientable high-dimensional image dataset.
gpt_response:
Many machine-learning tools try to “flatten” complicated data into a few coordinates, like making a map of a globe on a sheet of paper. But some shapes simply can’t be flattened without tearing or overlaps. Classic examples include the Möbius band, the Klein bottle, and the real projective plane—objects whose topology blocks any single, global set of Euclidean coordinates.

This paper proposes a workaround inspired by real-world atlases: instead of one global autoencoder, it trains several local autoencoders on overlapping regions of the data. Where two regions overlap, the model learns how to translate one region’s hidden coordinates into the other’s. Those translations act like the “glue” between map pages.

The key discovery: by checking whether these overlaps consistently preserve or flip orientation, the method can automatically decide if the underlying surface is orientable. Even with imperfect neural-network reconstructions, the authors prove this orientation test remains stable under clear error bounds. They also show the minimum number of local charts is controlled by a topological quantity called covering type.

Experiments on a sphere, Möbius band, Klein bottle, and projective-plane-like image data confirm accurate orientability detection.

title: Filters, topologies, the Rado graph and the Urysohn space
abstract: My work with Anatoly Vershik concerned automorphism groups of the Rado graph and homeomorphism groups of the Urysohn space. This paper contains some further thoughts on these issues, together with connections to topologies and filters on countable sets.
gpt_response:
Imagine shuffling an infinite set of points so symmetrically that no hidden “clumping” is preserved. Mathematicians call such a symmetry action *primitive*. Peter Cameron explores what happens when these symmetries also respect a way of saying which sets of points count as “nearby” (a topology).

A key idea is that topologies can be translated into simpler “direction” rules between points, and back again. With this, Cameron links two levels of symmetry: ordinary primitivity and a stronger version that forbids even these direction-like structures. He shows this matches classic separation properties of topologies (roughly: whether points can be told apart by open sets).

The paper then connects topologies to *filters*: collections of “large” sets closed under taking bigger sets and overlaps. A major result (simplified here) says that for countable sets, a symmetry group preserves a nontrivial topology exactly when it preserves a nontrivial filter.

Cameron also revisits Mekler’s condition, showing when a countable group can act as homeomorphisms of the “rational world” (a space shaped like the rationals). Finally, he studies graphs: the “neighborhood filter” built from vertex neighborhoods is nontrivial exactly when the graph contains the Rado (random) graph, making the Rado graph’s neighborhood filter universal among countable ones.

title: Comparison of Structure-Preserving Methods for the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes Equations
abstract: We develop structure-preserving discontinuous Galerkin methods for the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes equations with degenerate mobility. The proposed SWIPD-L and SIPGD-L methods incorporate parametrized mobility fluxes with edge-wise mobility treatments for enhanced coercivity-stability control. We prove coercivity for the generalized trilinear form and demonstrate optimal convergence rates while preserving mass conservation, energy dissipation, and the discrete maximum principle. Comparisons with existing SIPG-L and SWIP-L methods confirm similar stability. Validation on $hp$-adaptive meshes for both standalone Cahn-Hilliard and coupled systems shows significant computational savings without accuracy loss.
gpt_response:
When oil and water separate, they form swirling patterns and droplets. A popular math model for this is the Cahn–Hilliard equation, which tracks a “phase field” value that should always stay between −1 and 1 (think: pure fluid A to pure fluid B). A classic theorem says this bound holds in the ideal, continuous world—especially when the model uses a “degenerate mobility,” meaning mixing slows down near pure phases. But on a computer grid, many standard methods (including common finite-element and discontinuous-Galerkin approaches) can accidentally push values outside the physical range unless extra fixes are added.

This paper designs new structure-preserving discontinuous-Galerkin schemes, called SWIPD-L and SIPGD-L. Their key idea is a smarter way to handle mobility at the borders between grid cells, giving better control over numerical stability. The authors also prove a core stability property (coercivity) for their generalized formulation.

In simulations, the new methods match the expected accuracy in 2D and 3D, keep mass conserved, make energy steadily decrease, and maintain bounded phase values—both for phase separation alone and when coupled to fluid flow (Navier–Stokes). They also show that adaptive meshes and adaptive polynomial order can cut computational cost while keeping results reliable.

title: Compactness and Spectral Properties of Multiplier Operators in the Walsh System
abstract: We investigate compactness and spectral properties of multiplier operators associated with the Walsh system in the spaces $L^p[0,1]$, $1<p<\infty$. Building upon previously established criteria for boundedness of Walsh multipliers, we prove an exact compactness criterion in the $L^p\to L^p$ regime for all $1<p<\infty$(assuming boundedness of the multiplier), and also in the $L^p\to L^2$ regime for $2<p<\infty$. The key result states that compactness is equivalent to the condition $a_n\to 0$ for the multiplier symbol. We also examine in detail the point spectrum and derive strict spectral inclusions; in the Hilbert space case $p=2$ we obtain a complete description of the spectrum. For $p\neq 2$, we emphasize the limitations of transferring "diagonal" arguments and formulate results in a form that does not admit incorrect generalizations.
gpt_response:
Imagine doing “Fourier analysis,” but instead of smooth sine waves you use blocky, digital-looking waves that only flip between +1 and −1. Those are **Walsh functions**, built from the binary (base‑2) structure of numbers. They form a reliable building set for signals on the interval from 0 to 1, especially in many \(L^p\) spaces (a way mathematicians measure the size of functions).

This paper studies **Walsh multiplier operators**: you first break a function into Walsh “ingredients,” then you scale each ingredient by a chosen number \(a_n\), and finally you rebuild the function. The big question: when does this scaling process “squeeze” complicated inputs into a set that behaves like it’s almost finite-dimensional (mathematicians call this **compactness**)?

The authors prove a clean criterion: for any \(1<p<\infty\), the operator is compact **exactly when** the scaling numbers \(a_n\) go to zero. They show this by approximating the operator with finite truncations and controlling the leftover tail using Walsh versions of classic inequalities.

They also analyze the operator’s **spectrum** (its “special output scales”): in \(L^2\) it’s precisely the closure of \(\{a_n\}\), while for \(p\neq2\) they prove guaranteed inclusions without assuming Hilbert-space shortcuts.

title: Most probably trangle-free graphs
abstract: The celebrated Mantel's theorem states that any triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices contains at most $\left\lfloor n^2/4\right\rfloor$ edges. It is natural to ask how many triangles must exist in a graph with more than $\left\lfloor n^2/4\right\rfloor$ edges--a problem known as the Erdős-Rademacher problem. In this paper, we propose a probabilistic variant of this classic problem. Specifically, given an $n$-vertex graph $G$ with $\left\lfloor n^2/4\right\rfloor+i$ ($i>0$) edges, we choose the edges of $G$ independently with probability $p$, and the resulting new graph is triangle-free with a certain probability. Our goal is to maximize this probability by choosing $G$ appropriately. For the case where $G$ has $ \left\lfloor n^2/4\right\rfloor +1$ edges, we determine the exact maximum probability.
gpt_response:
Imagine a social network where a “triangle” means three people who all know each other. A classic result from 1907 (Mantel’s theorem) says: if you try to pack in as many friendships as possible while avoiding any such triangle, there’s a sharp maximum. Later work asked a tougher “supersaturation” question: once you add even a few extra friendships beyond that limit, how many triangles are you forced to create?

This paper flips the viewpoint in a probabilistic way. Start with a graph that has a fixed number of edges, then keep each edge independently with probability \(p\), deleting it otherwise. The authors ask: among all graphs with slightly “too many” edges, which one makes it *most likely* that the randomly thinned graph ends up triangle-free?

Their main result solves the first step beyond Mantel’s limit (exactly one extra edge). They prove the best strategy is to take the complete bipartite “no-triangle” graph and add the extra edge inside the larger side. They also give an exact formula for that maximum probability, using tools from probability inequalities (FKG/Harris) and a clever translation of triangles into a hypergraph independence problem. Open problems include handling two or more extra edges, where the best graph may depend on \(p\).

title: Ordered trees with distinguished children
abstract:
A new tree model is introduced based on ordered trees, by distinguishing exactly one child of each node that \emph{has} children. The basic enumeration leads to a cubic equation of the generating function. The extraction of its coefficients can be done using the Lagrange inversion formula. Various parameters that are commonly studied for ordered trees can also be addressed here, like degree of the root, number of leaves, number of old leaves, height, height of leftmost leaf, and pathlength. We go through these instances and leave further parameters to later research, by either the author or some readers. Dealing with cubic equations in a meaningful way requires some skills with Maple.
In a last section, ordered trees are replaced by marked ordered trees; they are then combined with the concept of distinguished children. Only the basic enumeration is provided, leaving further analysis to the future.
gpt_response:
Imagine a “family tree” drawn so the children of each node are ordered from left to right. Mathematicians love counting how many such ordered trees exist with a given number of nodes. Classic results connect these counts to famous number families like the Catalan and Narayana numbers, which track shapes and leaf counts.

This paper zooms in on a finer detail: among leaves, the leftmost child of a parent is called an “old” leaf, while the others are “young.” Instead of treating only the leftmost edge as special (an “unfair” rule), the author proposes a “fair” new model: **every non-leaf node must choose exactly one distinguished child edge**. That simple rule creates many more trees than the usual Catalan world.

Using generating functions (a bookkeeping tool) and a coefficient-extraction method called Lagrange inversion, the paper derives exact counting formulas, including how many trees have *n* nodes and *k* leaves. It then estimates typical features for large trees: they have slightly **more leaves**, are **a bit taller**, and the root tends to have **more children** than in classical ordered trees. Finally, it explores “marked” trees (some rightmost edges optionally flagged) and combines marking with distinguished children, producing a new sequence of counts and pointing to future work.

title: A class of bilateral weighted shift operators, and linear dynamics
abstract: This article aims to initiate a study of bilateral weighted backward shift operators defined on the spaces $\ell^p_{a,b}(\Omega_{r,R})$ and $c_{0,a,b}(\Omega_{r,R})$ which are Banach spaces of analytic functions on a suitable annulus in the complex plane, having a normalized Schauder basis of the form, $$ f_n(z):= (a_n+b_{n}z)z^{n},\hskip 0.5cm n\in \mathbb{Z}. $$ We obtain necessary and sufficient conditions for a weighted shift $B_w$ to be bounded, and find conditions so that $B_w$ is similar to a compact perturbation of a weighted shift on $\ell^p(\mathbb{Z})$. In addition, we study when $B_w$ is hypercyclic, supercyclic, and chaotic. It shown that the zero-one law of orbital limit points does not hold for $B_w$, which is in contrast to the case of weighted shifts on $\ell^p(\mathbb{Z})$. Most of our results are obtained using the matrix form of $B_w$.
gpt_response:
Imagine a machine that takes an infinite “two-sided” list of numbers and shifts every entry one step left, multiplying by a chosen weight each time. Mathematicians call this a *weighted backward shift*. This paper studies what happens when that machine acts not on plain lists, but on special spaces of analytic functions defined on a ring-shaped region (an annulus) in the complex plane.

The authors first build these function spaces using a carefully designed set of building blocks, like a custom basis. They prove that every function in the space has a unique expansion in this basis, and that “reading off” a function’s value at a point—or its Laurent-series coefficients—changes continuously as the function changes.

Next, they translate the shift operator into an infinite matrix and use it to find exact conditions for when the operator is bounded (doesn’t blow up sizes). Under extra assumptions, they show the operator is essentially a classical weighted shift plus a compact “small” correction, which lets them describe its essential spectrum as an annulus.

Finally, they give sharp criteria for when the shift is hypercyclic, mixing, supercyclic, or chaotic, and show a “zero–one law” about limit points sometimes holds—but can fail in these new spaces, with explicit counterexamples.

title: The regularity of the boundary of vortex patches for the quasi-geostrophic shallow-water equations
abstract: We prove the persistence of boundary smoothness of vortex patches for the quasi-geostrophic shallow-water (QGSW) equations. The QGSW equations generalize the Euler equations by including an additional parameter, the Rossby radius $\varepsilon^{-1}$, which modifies the relationship between the streamfunction and the (potential) vorticity. In addition, we prove that solutions of the QGSW equations converge locally in time to the corresponding Euler solutions as $\varepsilon \to 0$ in little Hölder spaces.
gpt_response:
Imagine tracking huge, swirling motions in the ocean or atmosphere. Mathematicians model this with the **quasi‑geostrophic shallow‑water (QGSW) equation**, where a quantity called *potential vorticity* is simply carried along by the flow—like dye drifting in water. The tricky part is that the flow speed is computed from vorticity using a special “influence rule” (a convolution kernel) built from **modified Bessel functions**, which makes the interaction slightly different from the classic 2D Euler fluid model.

This paper builds a full “it works and it’s unique” theory for QGSW. First, the authors prove **existence and uniqueness of smooth solutions** when the initial vorticity is reasonably regular, and also a **Yudovich‑style result** guaranteeing global well‑posedness even for merely bounded, compactly supported data (weak solutions). Their key technical move is to split the kernel’s derivative into a singular part that behaves like a standard fluid operator plus a gentler remainder.

They then tackle **vortex patches**: if vorticity starts as a sharp blob with a smooth boundary, the boundary stays smooth forever and the patch solution is unique. Finally, they prove that as the parameter ε shrinks to 0, **QGSW solutions converge to 2D Euler solutions** on a common time interval, rigorously justifying the link between the two models.

title: Are sparse graphs typically determined by their spectrum?
abstract:
We investigate whether it is typical for a sparse graph to be uniquely characterized by its adjacency spectrum up to isomorphism. Our first result shows that the giant component of an Erdős-Rényi graph is cospectral when the average degree is sufficiently small. The proof relies on the existence of a specific pendant tree, combined with a method by Schwenk that swaps trees to construct a cospectral mate.
It seems possible that pendant trees are essentially the only obstruction, meaning that the giant should become characterized by spectrum with high probability if one prunes these by considering the 2-core. The majority of the paper is devoted to theoretical and numerical evidence supporting this concept. Our main theorem in this direction establishes that local switching methods can not cause the 2-core to be cospectral. We also discuss R-cospectrality and rational cospectrality at fixed level.
gpt_response:
Can you recognize a network just by its “sound”? In graph theory, that “sound” is the list of eigenvalues of a graph’s adjacency matrix—numbers that act like a spectral fingerprint. Sometimes the fingerprint is unique, but sometimes two different graphs share it; these are called *cospectral mates*.

This paper asks what happens for *sparse* random graphs, where each possible edge appears with probability about λ/n. Such graphs typically contain one huge connected piece, the “giant component.” The authors show that when λ is small enough (around the scale of log n), the giant component almost surely has a cospectral mate. The reason is surprisingly simple: the giant often has small “dangling” trees attached. Swapping one special dangling tree for another can keep the spectrum unchanged, creating many non-isomorphic lookalikes—often exponentially many.

Then the authors strip away all dangling trees to study the tougher “2-core.” They prove that any *local* spectrum-preserving trick (including Godsil–McKay switching) fails there: with high probability, small switchings can’t produce a genuinely different graph. This supports a new conjecture that the 2-core is typically determined by its spectrum.

title: Generically sharp decay and blowing up at infinity for a weak null wave system
abstract:
We study a system of semilinear wave equations satisfying the weak null condition, which can be regarded as a simplified model for the Einstein vacuum equations. The main objective is to establish precise pointwise decay estimates, as both lower and upper bounds of decay, for small data solutions. Specifically, we show that the difference between the solution and its leading-order term is dominated by lower-order terms that decay faster in the retarded time variable $u=t-r$. Moreover, we prove that these pointwise decay estimates are sharp for a generic class of small initial data decaying sufficiently fast.
As applications of these estimates, we demonstrate that the energy of one component of the solution admits a lower bound that generically grows to infinity as $t\to +\infty$, which can be interpreted as ``blowing up at infinity." Furthermore, we verify that this component generically exhibits an energy cascade from high to low frequencies.
gpt_response:
Imagine two ripples moving through space, called ϕ and ψ, that don’t just travel—they also push on each other. This paper studies a simplified “toy model” of how gravitational waves behave in Einstein’s theory when written in a convenient coordinate choice (the wave gauge). The authors start with tiny initial disturbances placed on a curved, hyperbola-shaped “starting surface,” then track what happens forever into the future.

Their first big result: if the initial data are small enough, the waves exist for all time (no finite-time blow-up). Next, they pin down *exactly* how fast the waves fade, but the answer depends on where you look: an interior region and a far-away exterior region. A clever trick is to replace ψ by a modified field \bar{ψ} = ψ + ½ϕ², which makes the interactions easier to control and reveals the leading “tail” terms.

They also decompose the solution into spherical harmonic modes and show the slowest decay rates are typically unavoidable (“generically sharp”). Finally, even though ψ stays uniformly bounded in energy, ϕ shows an “energy cascade” and its overall energy grows without bound as time goes to infinity—blow-up, but only at infinity.

title: Error Analysis of Parameter Prediction via Gaussian Process Regression and Its Application to Weighted Jacobi Iteration
abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel theoretical framework for Gaussian process regression error analysis, leveraging a function-space decomposition. Based on this framework, we develop a weighted Jacobi iterative method that utilizes Gaussian process regression for parameter prediction and provide a corresponding convergence analysis. Moreover, the convergence conditions are designed to be compatible with other error bounds, enabling a more general analysis. Experimental results show that the parameters predicted based on Gaussian process regression significantly accelerate the convergence speed of Jacobi iterations.
gpt_response:
When computers solve huge systems of linear equations—like the ones that appear after turning a physics equation into a grid of numbers—they often use “iterative” methods: start with a guess, then repeatedly improve it. The classic Jacobi method is easy to run in parallel, but it can crawl. A faster variant, **weighted Jacobi**, adds a tuning knob (a relaxation weight). The catch: the best weight depends on hidden properties of the matrix, and for large problems those properties are too expensive to compute.

This paper proposes a workaround using **Gaussian Process Regression (GPR)**, a machine-learning tool that can predict good parameter values from a small set of training examples. The authors also build a new theory to **bound the prediction error**, by splitting the predicted function into a “fits-the-known-points” part plus a global correction. Crucially, they show how the GPR model’s own **uncertainty (variance)** can guarantee convergence: lower variance means safer, faster iteration.

In MATLAB tests on large grids from Laplace and convection–diffusion equations, GPR-chosen weights dramatically reduced iteration counts and runtime. Kernel choice mattered: a well-matched kernel lowered prediction error and sped up convergence even more.

title: Robust Distributed Nonconvex Optimization Enabling Communication Acceleration and Privacy Protection
abstract: This paper addresses a distributed nonconvex optimization problem over multi-agent networks, where each agent exchanges its local information solely with its neighbors. Given that most existing distributed nonconvex optimization algorithms are susceptible to information leakage during inter agent communications, we propose a Robust Proximal Primal dual algorithm, referred to as RPP, to enhance the security of information transmission. In contrast to many existing approaches that directly transmit local variables throughout the network, we introduce carefully designed random noises to obfuscate sensitive local information. This not only preserves privacy but also demonstrates the noise robustness of our proposed algorithm. We establish a sublinear rate at which RPP converges to a stationary solution. Moreover, by incorporating Chebyshev acceleration, an accelerated variant of RPP is developed and achieves the optimal communication complexity bound for the algorithms that allow for exchanging local deci sions at each iteration. The superior convergence performance of RPP is validated through a few numerical experiments, which also indicate that, within an appropriate range, the introduced perturbations do not impede the convergence speed of RPP.
gpt_response:
Modern systems—from power grids to wireless networks—often need many computers to jointly find the “best” settings. The catch: the math is usually *nonconvex*, meaning the landscape is full of hills and valleys, so finding a good solution is tricky. It gets even harder when computers can only talk to nearby neighbors on a sparse network, and when sharing raw values (like local model updates) could leak private information.

This paper proposes a new distributed method called **RPP** (Robust Proximal Primal-dual). Each device repeatedly improves its own guess using a carefully stabilized update rule, while also coordinating with neighbors so everyone gradually agrees. To speed up slow networks, the authors allow **multiple communication exchanges per iteration** and add a **momentum-like boost** to the coordination step.

For privacy, RPP uses an **encryption-by-noise** idea: devices send messages mixed with well-designed random perturbations that hide their true local variables. Unlike many earlier privacy tricks that slow learning or only reach “almost-correct” answers, RPP keeps a proven convergence speed. An accelerated version, **RPP-CA**, uses **Chebyshev acceleration** to cut communication and matches state-of-the-art efficiency. Experiments on distributed nonconvex logistic classification show faster progress and strong robustness even with privacy noise.

title: Topological entropy, mean dimension, and weakly equivalent flows
abstract:
In this paper, we mainly revisit a nice theory for topological entropy of weakly equivalent flows, which was originally investigated by Ohno in 1980. We will develop a new approach, being more straightforward and elementary than the measure-theoretic one provided by Ohno, to the theory for weak equivalence of flows, and as a novelty, we study both topological entropy and mean dimension with a highly unified process in relation to such objects.
In particular, for weakly equivalent flows without fixed points we recover Ohno's theorem for topological entropy relation with a substantially different method, and moreover, carry out an analogue within the framework of mean dimension; while for weakly equivalent flows with fixed points, our technique refines the procedure suggested in Ohno's construction, and strengthens Ohno's example with a view towards topological complexity of dynamical systems.
Essentially, our method is topological. For this purpose, we first introduce a modification to the definition of topological entropy, by relating a spanning set inside the state space to a finite set outside, which comes to be a tiny but key difference, via a map, and further, show that it leads eventually to the same value as the topological entropy. Although to an intermediate extent, the modified quantity generally does not coincide with the one appearing in the classical definition, it has some basic combinatorial feature, which not only applies flexibly to topological entropy, but also adapts directly to the mean dimension context. Using this alternative, we are allowed to re-establish and enrich Ohno's theory.
gpt_response:
Imagine watching two “movies” of motion on a space: points drift along paths over time. Mathematicians call this a **flow**. Two flows are **weakly equivalent** if a homeomorphism matches each path (orbit) in one movie to a path in the other, keeping the forward direction—yet it may let the clocks run at different speeds.

This paper revisits a classic question: does such orbit-matching preserve how “complicated” the motion is? Earlier work (Ohno) used probability-style tools. Here, the authors give **purely topological** proofs instead.

First, for flows **without fixed points** (no point stays forever still), they build a continuous “time-change” function that tells how much one clock must be sped up or slowed down along each orbit. From its minimum and maximum speeds, they prove both **topological entropy** (a chaos meter) and **mean dimension** (a complexity measure that can distinguish different kinds of “infinite complexity”) scale only by a constant factor between weakly equivalent flows.

A key technical contribution is a modified, more flexible definition of entropy using **finite partitions**, making estimates easier.

Finally, with **fixed points**, all bets are off: they construct weakly equivalent flows where one has **zero entropy** while the other has **infinite mean dimension**, showing orbit-matching can hide enormous complexity differences.

title: Just-infinite Jordan Banach algebras
abstract: By analogy with the well-established notions of just-infinite groups and just-infinite algebras, in particular $C^*$-algebras, we initiate a study of just-infinite $JB$-algebras, i.e. infinite dimensional $JB$-algebras for which all proper quotients are finite dimensional. We investigate the connections between a just-infinite $C^*$-algebra $A$ and its Jordan algebra $H(A,*)$ of self-adjoint elements. We also show that any just-infinite $JB$-algebra $J$ either is a infinite-dimensional spin factor or there exists a $C^*$-algebra $A$ and just-infinite norm-closed real $*$-subalgebras $A_1$ and $A_2$ of $A$ such that $H(A_1,*)\unlhd J \subseteq H(A_2,*).$
gpt_response:
Mathematicians often understand complicated algebraic “number systems” by looking at their *ideals*—special subsets that behave well under multiplication. This paper focuses on a striking extreme case called **just-infinite**: an algebra is infinite in size, but the moment you “collapse” it by any nonzero ideal, what remains becomes finite. (A familiar example is the polynomial ring in one variable.)

The authors study this idea in the world of **Jordan–Banach (JB) algebras**, which you can think of as algebras of “observable-like” self-adjoint operators equipped with a notion of distance (a norm). Their key method is to compare a JB algebra with the larger **C\*-algebra** it comes from, using the self-adjoint part and tracking how ideals correspond between the two.

Main results:  
1) The self-adjoint Jordan algebra inside a C\*-algebra is just-infinite **exactly when** the whole C\*-algebra is just-infinite.  
2) Every just-infinite JB algebra is actually a **JC algebra** (it can be realized concretely as norm-closed self-adjoint operators).  
3) Structurally, such JB algebras are either **infinite-dimensional spin factors** or sit inside the self-adjoint part of a **real associative just-infinite algebra**, with a just-infinite ideal embedded inside.

title: The global well-posedness of the multi-dimensional compressible Euler system with damping in the $L^p$ critical Besov spaces for $p<2$
abstract: In this paper, we study the Cauchy's problem of the compressible Euler system with damping and establish the global-in-time well-posedness in $L^p$-type critical Besov spaces for $1\leq p<2$. To achieve it, a new product estimate is established in $L^2$-$L^p$ hybrid Besov spaces.
gpt_response:
Imagine air moving through a sponge-like rock. The gas can speed up and compress, but the solid skeleton drags on it like friction, steadily slowing the flow. This paper analyzes a mathematical model for that situation: the “compressible Euler equations with linear damping,” where the drag force is proportional to the gas’s momentum.

The authors’ main goal is to prove that, if the initial disturbance is small enough, the model has a **unique solution that exists for all time**—even when the initial data are very “spiky” or concentrated. Earlier work could handle a wide range of settings, but mostly for a parameter choice corresponding to smoother data. Here they push into the harder case **p < 2**, which naturally includes more singular physical scenarios (think point-like sources).

To do this, they rewrite the equations using a new variable related to pressure (called enthalpy) and then split the motion into **large-scale** and **small-scale** patterns (low vs. high “frequencies”). Large scales are controlled using heat-like smoothing and damping effects; small scales require an energy-tracking method. A key technical contribution is a new way to estimate nonlinear “product” terms, which may also help study other systems like chemotaxis and Navier–Stokes.

title: On the Computation Rate of All-Reduce
abstract: In the All-Reduce problem, each one of the K nodes holds an input and wishes to compute the sum of all K inputs through a communication network where each pair of nodes is connected by a parallel link with arbitrary bandwidth. The computation rate of All-Reduce is defined as the number of sum instances that can be computed over each network use. For the computation rate, we provide a cut-set upper bound and a linear programming lower bound based on time (bandwidth) sharing over all schemes that first perform Reduce (aggregating all inputs at one node) and then perform Broadcast (sending the sum from that node to all other nodes). Specializing the two general bounds gives us the optimal computation rate for a class of communication networks and the best-known rate bounds (where the upper bound is no more than twice of the lower bound) for cyclic, complete, and hypercube networks.
gpt_response:
Training today’s giant AI models isn’t just about fast chips—it’s also about how quickly many machines can “talk” to each other. A key teamwork step is **All-Reduce**: every node starts with its own data value, and by exchanging messages, all nodes must end up knowing the **sum of everyone’s values**. This paper asks a fundamental question: given a network with links of different capacities (assumed perfectly reliable), what is the **best possible speed** for doing All-Reduce?

The authors measure speed using a communication-theory idea: how many sums can be completed per round of network use (allowing batching many sums together).

They prove two broad results. First, an **upper limit**: no algorithm can beat the capacity of the “tightest bottleneck cut” in the network—if you slice the network into two groups, the total bandwidth crossing that slice limits progress. Second, a **lower limit**: a practical strategy that first **collects** all values along a tree to one root (Reduce), then **spreads** the sum back along another tree (Broadcast). By mixing many such trees and optimizing the mix with **linear programming**, they maximize the guaranteed rate.

For common topologies (cycles, complete graphs, hypercubes), their bounds are the tightest known and are always within a factor of 2; for a special class of tree-combination networks, the bounds match exactly. Open problems remain, including the exact rate for small complete networks.

title: Analogue of the theta group $Γ_θ$
abstract: In this paper, we introduce higher level versions of the theta group $\Gamma_{\theta}.$ In particular, we treat level 3 and 4 versions of the theta group, $\Gamma_{\theta,3}$ and $\Gamma_{\theta,4}$ and prove that $\displaystyle F(\tau)=\eta \left(\frac{\tau-1}{3} \right) \eta\left(\frac{\tau+1}{3} \right)$ and $\displaystyle G(\tau)=\eta \left(\frac{\tau-1}{4} \right) \eta\left(\frac{\tau+1}{4} \right)$ are modular forms on $\Gamma_{\theta,3}$ and $\Gamma_{\theta,4}$ respectively. Moreover we compute their multiplier systems, $\nu_{F}$ and $\nu_{G}$.
gpt_response:
Some functions in math have a surprising “symmetry rule”: if you twist the input in certain precise ways, the output changes only by a predictable factor. These are called modular forms, and the allowed twists come from special 2×2 integer matrices (a “modular group”).  

This paper studies a famous subgroup called the *theta group* and then builds higher-level versions of it, labeled by an integer \(N\). The authors focus on two new groups, the level‑3 and level‑4 theta groups. They start from two classic building blocks, the Dedekind eta function and the theta function, which already have well-known symmetry behavior.  

Next, they construct two new eta-based functions: one using shifts and scaling by 3, and another by 4. The main job is to compute, case by case, the exact “phase factor” (multiplier system) that appears when these functions are transformed by matrices in the new groups. They show these multipliers behave like simple characters, then use their kernels (where the phase becomes 1) to generate many concrete examples of modular groups. Finally, they list explicit coset decompositions of the full modular group modulo the level‑3 and level‑4 theta groups, identifying key cusp points (∞ and −1).

title: Computing Invariants of Artin-Schreier Curves
abstract: We present an algorithmic framework for computing generators for the ring of invariants of an Artin-Schreier curve. We give explicit invariants for almost all Artin-Schreier curves of genus up to~8 in standard form, and for a handful of curves of higher genus.
gpt_response:
Imagine trying to tell when two complicated “shapes” are really the same, even if you stretch or re-label them. This paper tackles that problem for a special family of algebraic curves called **Artin–Schreier curves**, which live over number systems where counting wraps around a prime \(p\) (with \(p>2\)). These curves are famous because they often have many points and surprising symmetries, useful in areas like coding theory.

The authors focus on finding **invariants**: numerical fingerprints built from a curve’s coefficients that don’t change under allowed transformations. The big challenge is that the full symmetry group is infinite, making invariants hard to compute. Their key trick is to rewrite every curve into a carefully chosen **standard form** (by moving the biggest “singularities,” called poles, to special locations like \(0,1,\infty\)). This “rigidifies” the problem so that only a **finite** group of transformations remains.

With that reduction, they design general algorithms and implement them in **Magma** to compute invariant systems and describe moduli spaces (the “catalog” of all such curves) for genera \(5\)–\(8\) and beyond, extending earlier work for genera \(3\)–\(4\). They also report running times and numbers of generators, and release their code.

title: Potential Relation Between the Riemann Zeta Function and the Polynomial Function F of the Generalized Erdős--Straus Conjecture, Subject to its Analytic Continuation
abstract: In this article, we explore a natural extension of the quadratic parametrization introduced in our previous work. By replacing the integer n by n^s (s ∈ ℝ, s > 1) and allowing the parameters to be real, we obtain for each n ≥ 1 a decomposition k/n = 1/x_s(n) + 1/y_s(n) + 1/z_s(n) with x_s(n), y_s(n), z_s(n) ∈ ℝ^+. Summing this equality over all integers brings forth the Riemann zeta function. Subject to an analytic continuation of the quantities x_s(n), y_s(n), z_s(n) to complex values of s, one would obtain a new function (|G_k(s)|) satisfying G_k(s) = k ζ(s), thus establishing a deep connection between the structure of the conjecture and the zeros of ζ.
gpt_response:
In 1948, mathematicians Paul Erdős and Ernst Strauss posed a deceptively simple puzzle: can every whole number \(n\ge 2\) make the fraction “4 divided by \(n\)” split neatly into three “unit fractions” (fractions with 1 on top)? Variants by Sierpiński (using 5) and a broader version for any fixed \(k\ge 4\) are still unproven, even though computers have checked the original case up to about \(10^{17}\).

This paper offers a unifying trick. Instead of searching directly for the three fractions, the authors build a special expression \(F\) depending on two chosen parameters. They show: finding the three-fraction split is equivalent to making \(F\) land exactly on a perfect square. When \(F\) hits zero, the solution becomes especially simple (two of the fractions match), and such “zero cases” appear surprisingly often.

Then comes the bold leap: replace \(n\) by \(n^s\) (with real \(s>1\)) and allow real-number parameters. Summing the resulting identities over all \(n\) naturally produces the famous Riemann zeta function. If this construction can be extended to complex \(s\), the new function would share the same zeros as zeta—hinting at a possible new angle on the Riemann Hypothesis.

title: Ribbon concordance and fibered predecessors, II: the general case
abstract: The first and third authors recently proved that for each knot K ⊂ S³ there are only finitely many hyperbolic fibered knots which are ribbon concordant to K. In this paper, we remove the hyperbolic constraint, proving that every knot in S³ has only finitely many fibered predecessors under ribbon concordance. The key new input is an inequality relating the knot Floer homology of a generalized satellite knot with that of its companion, proved via the immersed curves formulation of bordered Heegaard Floer homology, which should be of independent interest. Our work, together with results of Kojima--McShane, also leads to an explicit upper bound on the Gromov norm of the complement of any fibered predecessor of a knot K ⊂ S³, in terms of the arc index and genus of K.
gpt_response:
Imagine lining up knots by a “can be simplified into” relation called **ribbon concordance**. Recent work showed this relation is a true partial order, and mathematicians suspect you can’t keep stepping downward forever. This paper backs an even stronger idea: for any knot \(K\), there are only **finitely many** simpler knots \(J\) that can ribbon-concord into it—at least when those \(J\) are **fibered knots** (knots whose complements look like stacked copies of a surface).

Earlier results proved finiteness only for a special geometric class (“hyperbolic”). The new paper removes that restriction by tackling the tricky “satellite” situation, where a knot is built by wrapping a pattern around another knot (the “companion”).

The key new tool is an inequality from **knot Floer homology** (a powerful knot invariant): for satellite constructions with nonzero winding, the companion’s Floer homology can’t be larger than the satellite’s. Using branched covers and a curve-based version of Floer theory, the authors bound the complexity of possible companions and the “stretching” behavior of the knot’s surface map. They also show that simple diagram data (genus and arc index) gives an upper bound on the geometric complexity (Gromov norm) of any fibered predecessor’s complement.

title: Comparison of Topologies on Homotopy Groups with Subgroup Topology Viewpoint
abstract: By introducing various topologies on the homotopy groups of a topological space, some researchers make these well known notions in algebraic topology more useful and powerful. In this paper, first we recall and review some known topologies on homotopy groups. Then by reviewing some famous subgroups of homotopy groups and using the concept of subgroup topology, we intend to compare these topologies in order to present some results on topologized homotopy groups.
gpt_response:
Imagine trying to catalog all the ways you can “wrap” a rubber sheet around a shape without tearing it. Mathematicians do this with *homotopy groups*, which record different kinds of loops and higher‑dimensional “loops” (like spheres) in a space. But the authors ask a subtler question: can we also talk about which of these wrapping patterns are “close” to each other?

Their paper surveys many existing ways to put a notion of closeness (a *topology*) on these homotopy groups—such as the whisker, compact‑open quotient, tau, lim, Spanier, thick/weak thick Spanier, shape, and pseudometric approaches. They also review several important subgroups built from “tiny” loops that can be squeezed into arbitrarily small neighborhoods, plus Spanier‑type subgroups built from open covers. A new player is introduced: the *path Spanier subgroup*, based on covers chosen along paths.

Using a general “subgroup‑based” method for building topologies, they create new topologies from these subgroups and prove a detailed hierarchy showing which topologies are finer or coarser. They also give conditions when inequalities become equalities, including a key result: a space is “n‑semilocally H‑connected” exactly when the subgroup *H* is open in the whisker topology.

title: Measuring the Infinite: An Expository Journey Through Interpolation Theory, Lorentz Spaces, and Dispersive PDEs
