abstract: This expository article explores the vital role of interpolation theory and Lorentz spaces in the rigorous analysis of partial differential equations (PDEs). While classical Lebesgue spaces (Lₚ) successfully measure the magnitude of functions, they frequently fail to bound linear and non-linear evolution operators at critical endpoints of p = 1 or p = ∞ because they conflate a function's amplitude with its spatial spread. To resolve this analytic bottleneck, we introduce distribution functions and decreasing rearrangements, culminating in the construction of Lorentz spaces (Lₚ,ₚ). By utilizing the Complex (Riesz–Thorin) and Real (Peetre's K-functional) methods of interpolation, these highly sensitive intermediate spaces act as geometric bridges between endpoint extremes. We apply this framework to two distinct physical models: deriving the continuous smoothing decay of the parabolic Heat equation, and establishing the foundational dispersive Strichartz estimates for the hyperbolic free Schrödinger equation. Ultimately, interpolation theory is shown to be the essential mathematical language for quantifying both thermal diffusion and quantum dispersion.
gpt_response:
When physicists model heat spreading through a metal rod or a quantum wave packet drifting apart, they often end up with partial differential equations. Mathematicians then ask a practical question: if you start with a certain “shape” of heat or probability, how big can it get later?

For a long time, the main measuring tools were the familiar “Lp spaces,” which can track total amount, energy, or the highest peak. But many important operators behave nicely in the middle of this scale and suddenly misbehave at the extremes—like an averaging tool called the Hardy operator, which works for most cases but breaks at the endpoint that represents total mass.

This paper explains how interpolation theory fixes that gap. The key upgrade is Lorentz spaces, which separate “how tall” a spike is from “how widely” it spreads by sorting function values from largest to smallest. Using two interpolation methods (one complex, one real), the authors show sharper bounds for the heat equation’s smoothing and for the Schrödinger equation’s dispersion—capturing even borderline, highly spiky data that ordinary tools miss.

title: Deep ensemble graph neural networks for probabilistic cosmic-ray direction and energy reconstruction in autonomous radio arrays
abstract:
Using advanced machine learning techniques, we developed a method for reconstructing precisely the arrival direction and energy of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays from the voltage traces they induced on ground-based radio detector arrays.
In our approach, triggered antennas are represented as a graph structure, which serves as input for a graph neural network (GNN). By incorporating physical knowledge into both the GNN architecture and the input data, we improve the precision and reduce the required size of the training set with respect to a fully data-driven approach. This method achieves an angular resolution of 0.092° and an electromagnetic energy reconstruction resolution of 16.4% on simulated data with realistic noise conditions.
We also employ uncertainty estimation methods to enhance the reliability of our predictions, quantifying the confidence of the GNN's outputs and providing confidence intervals for both direction and energy reconstruction. Finally, we investigate strategies to verify the model's consistency and robustness under real life variations, with the goal of identifying scenarios in which predictions remain reliable despite domain shifts between simulation and reality.
gpt_response:
When an ultra‑energetic cosmic ray slams into Earth’s atmosphere, it triggers a domino effect of particles called an “air shower.” As this shower races along, it also flashes out radio waves—mainly because Earth’s magnetic field bends charged particles, and because the shower carries a slight extra negative charge. Experiments like GRAND plan to listen for these radio signals with huge fields of antennas, hoping to pinpoint not only cosmic rays but also rare neutrinos.

The challenge: each event triggers a different number of antennas in an irregular pattern, and classic methods that fit a simple “flat” wavefront can become biased, especially for very slanted showers or noisy data.

This study trains a graph neural network (a model built for scattered sensor networks) on 25,000 detailed simulations, including realistic antenna electronics and background noise. The model starts with a fast physics estimate of direction, then learns systematic corrections from timing “leftovers,” plus antenna positions and signal strengths. Using an ensemble of 12 networks, it reconstructs arrival direction more precisely than the classic fit (about 0.09° vs 0.16°) and estimates shower energy with ~16% resolution, while also providing well‑calibrated uncertainty ranges. Direction stays robust even when conditions change; energy is more sensitive to missing or miscalibrated antennas.

title: Extreme Emission Line Galaxies in CEERS Are Powered by Star Formation, not AGN
abstract: We present a spectroscopic study of photometrically identified extreme emission-line galaxies (EELGs) with observed-frame equivalent widths (EWs) >5000 A of either H alpha or H beta + [OIII] in the CEERS legacy deep field utilizing JWST NIRSpec spectroscopy from the CAPERS, RUBIES, THRILS and CEERS surveys. This master sample allows for performance tests of photometric selections and unveils what types of sources, either AGN or young star formation, were producing excessive ionizing radiation in the early Universe. We identify AGN through broad H alpha emission-lines and report 6 new broad-line AGN at 3.5<z<7 identified by the deep (~8 hr) G395M THRILS survey. We investigate the photometrically selected EELGs in a color-color plot designed for ``Little Red Dot'' selection and demonstrate that it effectively removes AGN with non-extreme lines from the sample. EELGs with and without broad lines show similar optical line ratios. We compare emission-line morphology to EWs and continuum morphologies and find that [OIII] morphology is more compact at higher EW. ~10% of photometrically selected EELGs have broad Balmer lines, jumping to 35% in deep spectroscopy which indicates a significant fraction of photometrically selected EELGs may host AGN. However, many AGN selected as EELGs have incorrectly high photometric EWs. For sources with extreme emission-line EWs that pass our photometric criteria and host an AGN, we find that the narrow H alpha component dominates over the broad, especially in the highest-EW sources. This implies that even when an AGN is present, it does not dominate the extreme emission.
gpt_response:
In the young universe—when it was only a few hundred million years old—astronomers keep finding galaxies whose light is “spiked” by incredibly bright glow from hot gas. These are called extreme emission-line galaxies, and their signals are so strong they can even distort James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) color images.

The big mystery is what powers that glow: furious bursts of newborn stars, or feeding supermassive black holes (active galactic nuclei, AGN)? To find out, the team took JWST/NIRSpec spectra of 181 previously “photometry-picked” extreme galaxies in the CEERS field, then looked for a telltale AGN sign: hydrogen lines that are unusually broadened by fast-moving gas near a black hole. They also stacked many spectra together to reveal faint features.

They identified 23 broad-line AGN (including 6 newly discovered in deep THRILS observations), showing that deeper, sharper spectra uncover AGN missed before. But crucially, in the truly most extreme galaxies, the narrow (star-formation-like) emission usually dominates—even when an AGN is present. Classic line-ratio tests also become unreliable at these early times, because young galaxies have low metals and highly energized gas that can mimic AGN-like fingerprints.

title: A precessing jet from a supermassive black hole: multi-wavelength observations of S5 1044+71
abstract: The bright gamma-ray blazar S5 1044+71 has been identified as showing very significant quasi-periodic oscillations in the Fermi-LAT data in recent studies, with a periodicity of about 3 years. With the completion of a new gamma-ray cycle, we aim to revisit the periodicity in Fermi-LAT data, and analyze all available multi-wavelength (MWL) data to search for possible correlations and time-lags. These observations will be used to test for the compatibility of the observed periodicity with a precessing jet from the supermassive black hole. We analyze data from Fermi-LAT, NuSTAR, Swift, AstroSat, ASAS-SN, ZTF, Pan-STARRS, and NEOWISE. In addition we present an analysis from historical observations from Palomar and Pulkovo. Single-band spectral variability, MWL correlations, and cross-correlations are computed. We then model the Fermi-LAT light curve with a precessing jet model, providing constraints on the geometry of the system and providing the evolution of the Doppler factor with time. The latter is used as input for MWL fitting of the spectral energy distribution. We confirm previous claims on the existence of a periodic gamma-ray signal. We detect significant spectral variability in gamma-ray, X-rays, and optical/UV data. We detect significant correlation between low-energy (infrared/optical/ultraviolet) data and gamma-rays, with a correlation index of about 1; the correlation between X-rays and gamma-ray is milder, with a correlation index of about 0.3. We do not detect any significant time-lag between bands. The Fermi-LAT light curve is successfully fit by a precessing jet model. The fit to the spectral energy distributions indicate that S5 1044+71 is a typical blazar, in which the gamma-ray emission is located beyond the broad-line region. All MWL observations we present in this work are consistent with the existence of a precessing relativistic jet from the supermassive black hole.
gpt_response:
Far beyond the Milky Way, some galaxies hide supermassive black holes that shoot out near‑light‑speed jets. When one of these jets points almost straight at Earth, we see a “blazar,” often blazing in gamma rays.

This study zooms in on the blazar S5 1044+71. Using 17 years of Fermi gamma‑ray monitoring plus X‑ray (NuSTAR, Swift, AstroSat), optical/UV (Swift and surveys like ZTF and ASAS‑SN), infrared (NEOWISE), and even old photographic plates, the team tracked how its brightness changes across the spectrum.

They confirm a repeating pattern: major gamma‑ray outbursts return about every three years, including a new peak arriving right when earlier work predicted. Optical and UV brighten almost at the same time as gamma rays, with no clear delay, while X‑rays correlate more weakly. The “color” of the light also shifts: gamma rays and X‑rays get harder when brighter, but optical/UV gets softer.

The best explanation is geometric: the jet slowly precesses like a wobbling spinning top, so its aim—and the boosting of its light—changes periodically. Modeling suggests the main emission region sits beyond the galaxy’s broad‑line region, making S5 1044+71 a promising target for future very‑high‑energy gamma‑ray telescopes.

title: A White Dwarf Tidal Disruption by an Intermediate-Mass Black Hole as the Progenitor of Ultra-long GRB 250702B
abstract: The recent detection of GRB 250702B, the longest gamma-ray burst observed to date with prompt emission lasting $\sim 2.5\times 10^4$ seconds, challenges the conventional collapsar model. Its remarkable features--including an extraordinary X-ray flare at $\sim 1.3$ days post-detection, a late-time transition from steep to shallow decay in the X-ray afterglow, and hard spectra extending from keV to MeV energies--point to a novel progenitor. Here we show that these multiwavelength signatures can be consistently explained by a relativistic jet powered by successive partial tidal disruptions of a white dwarf (WD) by an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH). By modeling the time-dependent accretion rate from repeated partial disruptions and the resulting jet evolution, we show that the external forward and reverse shocks account for the long-term X-ray, near-infrared, and radio afterglow, whereas the luminous X-ray flare originates from internal energy dissipation caused by collisions between fast and slow relativistic ejecta associated with the final complete disruption. Our findings establish IMBH-WD tidal disruption events as a viable engine for ultra-long GRBs.
gpt_response:
Gamma-ray bursts are usually split into “short” and “long” events, powered by narrow, near–light-speed jets from extreme cosmic engines. But GRB 250702B broke the rules: its gamma-ray activity lasted about seven hours—the longest ever seen—yet it still showed the telltale signs of a powerful jet.

This study argues that the engine wasn’t a collapsing massive star. Instead, a white dwarf likely skimmed past an intermediate-mass black hole and got repeatedly “shaved” by tidal forces. Each close pass stripped off gas that later fell back and fed the black hole, keeping the jet running far longer than normal. The authors calculated how this feeding rate changes over time, then simulated how the jet’s blast waves plow into surrounding gas to produce the long-lived afterglow seen in X-rays, infrared, and radio.

One dramatic X-ray flare about 1.3 days later couldn’t be explained by those external blast waves. The team reproduced it by adding collisions between faster and slower blobs inside the jet—an internal crash that briefly supercharged the emission. Together, the model matches both the light curves and the hard X-ray-to–gamma-ray spectra.

title: Dyson spheres on H-R diagram
abstract: The construction of Dyson spheres, megastructures designed to capture the total radiative output of stars, can be one of the most compelling techno-signature scenarios for advanced extraterrestrial civilizations. By considering equilibrium temperatures, we investigate the luminosities and fluxes of Dyson spheres built around two promising classes of host stars: white dwarfs and red M-dwarfs. Using radiative balance arguments and representative stellar parameters, we compute the temperature-radius relationship for full energy interception and place these hypothetical structures on the Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram to assess their observational signatures. Our results show that Dyson spheres around white dwarfs produce cooler and fainter blackbody emissions, peaking in the near- to mid-infrared, while those around M-dwarfs radiate more strongly but at longer wavelengths. In both cases, the equilibrium temperature decreases as R_ D^-1/2, while the total luminosity and observed bolometric flux remain fixed by the stellar output. These findings highlight the astrophysical suitability of low-luminosity stars as Dyson sphere hosts and provide practical constraints for future techno-signature searches using infrared surveys.
gpt_response:
Imagine wrapping a star in a giant energy-collecting shell—a “Dyson sphere,” first proposed by physicist Freeman Dyson. The big idea is simple: the structure would soak up starlight and then dump the same energy back into space as “waste heat,” mostly as infrared glow. That glow’s color depends mainly on how big the sphere is: a larger sphere spreads the heat over more area, so it runs cooler and shines at longer infrared wavelengths.

This paper explores a wide range of Dyson-sphere sizes around two especially interesting kinds of stars: red M-dwarfs and white dwarfs. M-dwarfs are the Galaxy’s most common stars and can last for trillions of years, offering long-term power. White dwarfs are small, faint stellar remnants with very “clean” light, so any extra infrared emission would stand out.

The authors calculate expected temperatures, brightness, and infrared signals, then plot where these spheres would land on a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram—far from normal stars, in a cool, dim region. They argue that surveys like WISE and the James Webb Space Telescope could search nearby stars for smooth infrared “excess” that doesn’t look like dusty disks, guiding future techno-signature hunts.

title: Efficient training of generative models from multireference simulations and its application to the design of Dy complexes with large magnetic anisotropy
abstract: Generative machine learning models can potentially provide direct access to novel and relevant portions of the full chemical space, overcoming the cost of systematic sampling. However, the training of these models generally requires a large amount of data, often precluding the use of expensive high-level ab initio simulations for this task. The generation of coordination compounds of Dy with large magnetic anisotropy represents a topical example, where multireference simulations of large molecules are necessary to perform reliable predictions. Here, we show that a semi-supervised chemically-inspired training-by-proxy of generative variational autoencoders can reduce the cost associated with building a training set from multireference simulations by two orders of magnitude. We illustrate the power of this approach by generating 100s of new organic ligands for Dy(III) pentagonal bipyramidal complexes exhibiting record values of magnetic anisotropy, while starting from datasets as small as 1k multireference calculations. This work thus paves the way to the computational generation of molecules as complex coordination compounds with target electronic and magnetic properties.
gpt_response:
Imagine trying to design a “molecular magnet” that could one day store information like a tiny hard drive. The best candidates, called single‑molecule magnets, often use a dysprosium (Dy) atom surrounded by organic “ligands.” Their magnetic stability depends on delicate electronic energy spacings—numbers that usually require very expensive quantum‑chemistry simulations, so researchers can only test a few molecules at a time.

This study shows a shortcut. The team built a generative AI model (a variational autoencoder) that learns how ligands are written as SMILES strings and then invents new, chemically valid ligands. To avoid needing huge amounts of costly Dy simulations, they used semi‑supervised learning: the AI trains on many unlabeled ligands, while only a small subset has detailed labels.

Even smarter, the final system (GAUSS‑II) is guided mostly by cheap “proxy” properties of the ligand’s binding atom—like its local charge and polarizability—computed with faster methods. Those proxies naturally line up with the expensive magnetic energy gaps, letting the model target high‑performance designs. With only about 1,000 high‑level Dy calculations, GAUSS‑II generated new Dy complexes with record‑level predicted magnetic behavior, cutting training cost by roughly 100×.

title: Extended Ashkin-Teller transition in two coupled frustrated Haldane chains
abstract: We report an extremely rich ground state phase diagram of two spin-1 Haldane chains frustrated with a three-site exchange and coupled by the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg interaction on a zig-zag ladder. A particular feature of the phase diagram is the extended quantum phase transition in the Ashkin-Teller universality class that separates the plaquette phase, which spontaneously breaks translation symmetry, and the uniform disordered phase. The former is connected to the Haldane phase, stabilized by large inter-chain coupling, via the topological Gaussian transition. Upon decreasing the inter-chain interactions, this intermediate disorder phase vanishes, giving place to a dimerized phase separated from the plaquette phase on one side via a non-magnetic Ising transition and from the Haldane phase on the other side by a topological weak first-order transition. Finally, in the limit of two decoupled chains, we recover a quantum critical point that corresponds to two copies of the Wess-Zumino-Witten $\mathrm{SU(2)}_2$ criticality with a total central charge $c=3$.
gpt_response:
Imagine a line of tiny quantum magnets (“spins”) arranged as a zig‑zag ladder. Depending on how strongly each spin talks to its neighbors—and even to pairs of neighbors through a special three‑spin interaction—the whole system can settle into very different collective “patterns,” or phases.

In this work, researchers map out the ground‑state phase diagram of a spin‑1 zig‑zag ladder with nearest‑neighbor, next‑nearest‑neighbor, and three‑site couplings. Using a powerful numerical method called DMRG, they diagnose phases by looking at bond‑correlation patterns (valence‑bond pictures) and by using quantum entanglement as a fingerprint.

They find a topological Haldane phase (with protected edge spins), a translation‑breaking plaquette phase with a four‑site repeating pattern (ℤ₄ order), and—crucially—an unexpected uniform, topologically trivial “in‑between” phase. The boundary between this uniform phase and the ℤ₄ plaquette phase forms an extended Ashkin–Teller critical line, confirmed by entanglement‑based central charge and scaling of the order parameter and correlation length. They also identify a separate Ising‑type transition (ℤ₂ to ℤ₄) and regions where transitions become abrupt (first‑order).

title: Testing the Weak Gravity Conjecture via Gravitational Lensing, Black Hole Shadows, and Barrow Thermodynamics in F(R)-Euler-Heisenberg (A)dS Black Holes
abstract: We investigate the interplay of the Weak Gravity Conjecture (WGC) and the Weak Cosmic Censorship Conjecture (WCCC) in $F(R)$-Euler-Heisenberg black holes in Anti-de Sitter and de Sitter backgrounds. The solution is characterized by the electric charge $q$, the $F(R)$ deviation $f_{R_0}$, the Euler--Heisenberg coupling $\lambda$, and the constant scalar curvature $R_0$. We establish a universal entropy--extremality relation that provides thermodynamic evidence for the WGC independently of $f_{R_0}$ and $R_0$. Photon sphere analysis from both geodesic and topological perspectives confirms the simultaneous compatibility of the WGC and WCCC, with the Euler--Heisenberg coupling restoring photon spheres in the naked singularity regime. Gravitational lensing in the strong- and weak-deflection limits reveals that the photon sphere radius is independent of the cosmological background while the critical impact parameter nearly doubles in de Sitter. Black hole shadow images under isotropic accretion are constructed. Within the Barrow entropy framework, we uncover van der Waals-type phase transitions and analyze Joule-Thomson expansion, identifying the small black hole phase as the WGC-compatible thermodynamic regime accessible via isenthalpic cooling.

This paper explores that idea using a special kind of **charged black hole** built from two upgrades to Einstein’s theory: a modified gravity model called **F(R)** and a nonlinear version of electromagnetism inspired by **Euler–Heisenberg** quantum effects.

The authors first derive the black hole’s basic features: how many horizons it can have (two, one “extremal,” or none—meaning a naked singularity), plus its temperature, mass (using the AMD method), and a consistent “first law” of black‑hole thermodynamics.

Next, they test the **Weak Gravity Conjecture (WGC)** with a clever deformation trick: turning up the nonlinear‑electromagnetism strength slightly. They find a universal result—this quantum correction **lowers the extremal mass while increasing entropy**, making extremal black holes unstable, as WGC expects.

They then study **photon spheres** (where light can orbit) and show they remain unstable and outside the horizon across allowed parameters, supporting **cosmic censorship** too. Finally, they connect theory to observations by predicting changes in **gravitational lensing** and **black‑hole shadows** (like EHT images), and by analyzing phase transitions and cooling/heating behavior using **Barrow’s “fractal” entropy**.

title: Quantum Oppenheimer-Snyder Black Holes with a Cloud of Strings Surrounded by Perfect Fluid Dark Matter
abstract: In this study, we examine quantum Oppenheimer-Snyder black holes (BHs) embedded within a cloud of strings and immersed in perfect fluid dark matter. Also, beginning with the underlying spacetime geometry, we determine how quantum corrections, string cloud contributions, and dark matter effects alter the geometrical structure and physical characteristics of the BH. Also, the optical behavior is investigated via a systematic analysis of the photon sphere and the associated BH shadow, emphasizing possible observational features capable of differentiating this configuration from classical models. We also analyze the motion of test particles, focusing on how surrounding matter components affect trajectories, stability conditions, and effective potentials. Scalar field perturbations are considered to investigate the BH response to external excitations and to extract information regarding its dynamical properties. In this case, the thermodynamic behavior of the system is studied, including the role of string clouds and dark matter in modifying BH thermodynamic quantities. Also, the obtained results present a unified description of the combined effects of quantum corrections, nonstandard matter sources, and BH physics, with potential relevance for both observational constraints and theoretical modeling of compact objects.

Black holes are usually described by Einstein’s general relativity, but today’s ultra-sharp observations—like the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) images of M87* and Sagittarius A*—let scientists test whether real black holes might deviate slightly from the textbook picture.

This study builds a “modified” black hole model by combining three ingredients: (1) quantum corrections to the classic Oppenheimer–Snyder collapse idea, (2) a surrounding “cloud of strings” (a hypothetical web of string-like matter), and (3) perfect-fluid dark matter, meant to mimic dark matter’s local influence near the hole. The authors first examine how these additions reshape the black hole’s horizon and the strength of spacetime curvature, confirming the central singularity stays hidden behind an event horizon.

Next, they track how light and matter move: the photon sphere (where light can orbit), the predicted shadow size, photon paths, and the stability of particle orbits such as the inner edge of accretion disks. They also study how ripples in a simple scalar field would “ring” around the hole, linking to quasinormal-mode signatures.

Finally, they compute temperature, entropy, heat capacity, and free energy, finding possible phase transitions and remnant-like behavior. Turning off all three effects recovers the standard Schwarzschild black hole.

title: Quantum corrected thermodynamics and horizon quantization of the Reissner--Nordström black hole
abstract: In this letter, we develop a unified semiclassical framework for the thermodynamics and quantization of the Reissner--Nordström (RN) black hole (BH) based on the Misner--Sharp--Hernandez (MSH) mass. Treating the quasi-local horizon energies as the relevant thermodynamic variables, we formulate a horizon-by-horizon first law and Smarr relation. Using a reduced phase-space quantization, we obtain a discrete MSH mass spectrum for both horizons, which reproduces the minimal entropy spacing. Quantum transitions between adjacent levels yield Planck-scale corrections to the Hawking temperatures and a universal logarithmic contribution to the entropy, consistent with independent approaches to quantum gravity. We encode these corrections into a quantum-deformed RN geometry via a simple multiplicative factor that preserves the classical horizon positions while reproducing the corrected surface gravities. The associated effective stress tensor behaves as a conserved vacuum-polarization source with characteristic $r^{-4}$ falloff and a small trace, providing a compact representation of semiclassical backreaction. The deformation slightly lowers both horizon temperatures, weakens the inner-horizon instability, and induces tiny shifts in photon-sphere and shadow observables for macroscopic BHs.
gpt_response:
Black holes aren’t just cosmic vacuum cleaners—they also behave like hot objects that can “glow” through Hawking radiation. This paper tackles a charged black hole (the Reissner–Nordström type), which has two horizons: an outer one and a hidden inner one. The authors use a practical way to define the energy near each horizon, called the Misner–Sharp–Hernandez mass, and show that **each horizon obeys its own local version of the first law of thermodynamics**, including a “work” term coming from the electric field. They also recover the matching scaling rule (Smarr relation) for both horizons, even though the inner horizon has a **negative temperature** because its gravity points the “wrong” way.

Next, they apply a streamlined quantization method: by rewriting the horizon dynamics in a form similar to two simple oscillators, they find that **each horizon’s energy comes in discrete steps**, implying a minimal spacing in entropy. Studying jumps between neighboring levels predicts small quantum corrections: both horizon temperatures drop slightly, and the entropy gains a universal **logarithmic extra term**, consistent with other quantum-gravity arguments. Finally, they build an effective, gently modified spacetime geometry that reproduces these corrections and corresponds to a tiny vacuum-polarization “quantum stress” that fades rapidly with distance.

title: WKB-like approach to the Unruh temperature for arbitrary acceleration
abstract: In this work we study the Unruh temperature as arising from tunneling through a barrier for an observer in flat Minkowski spacetime with arbitrary acceleration $a(t)$. For the defining case of constant acceleration $a(t) = a_0$, the Unruh temperature (W. Unruh, Phys. Rev. D 14, 870 (1976)) is given by $k_b\,T_U =\tfrac{\hbar\,a_0}{2\,\pi\,c}$. Extending the work of de Gill et al. (A. de Gill, D. Singleton, V. Akhmedova and T. Pilling, Am. J. Phys. 78, 685 (2010)) we generalize the gravitational WKB approach to derive the Unruh temperature for arbitrary acceleration. We show that the often employed Schwarzschild-like form of the flat metric is not appropriate for the WKB calculation with an arbitrary $a(t)$, and instead derive a generalized Unruh temperature for the generalized Rindler metric where $a_0\to a(t)$. We derive a generalization of the Rindler coordinates appropriate for arbitrary $a(t)$, and stress the importance of the role of the integrated acceleration $\chi(t) = \int^t dt'\,a(t')$, which can also act as a temporal coordinate. We explore several non-trivial examples of $a(t)$ and their generalized Unruh temperatures. We additionally develop an approximation to the Unruh temperature for small deviations away from constant acceleration by the standard approach of considering the negative frequency content of a purely positive frequency plane wave of an inertial observer, as measured by the co-moving arbitrarily accelerated observer. Lastly, we develop and explicit coordinate transformation between the arbitrarily accelerated observer and conformal coordinates, where the plane wave structure of the solutions of the wave equation is readily transparent, and analogous to the form for the inertial observer.
gpt_response:
Imagine floating in empty space while firing a rocket. In 1976, physicist Bill Unruh predicted something bizarre: if you accelerate steadily, “empty” space won’t look empty anymore. Your detector would click as if it were sitting in a warm bath of particles—while an unaccelerated observer still sees a perfect vacuum. This Unruh effect is closely tied to Hawking radiation from black holes, because hovering near a black hole’s horizon also requires constant acceleration.

This paper asks a new question: what if the acceleration isn’t constant—what if it changes with time? The author builds a generalized “accelerated coordinate system” for any acceleration history and shows the key quantity is the *accumulated* acceleration over time.

To predict the temperature an accelerating observer would measure, the paper extends a popular “tunneling” method (often used for black holes), carefully including both space and time contributions when crossing the horizon-like boundary. The result: the usual Unruh temperature is modified by a correction factor that depends on the whole acceleration profile.

Two example motions are tested (a short acceleration burst and a smooth tanh-shaped flip), and the predictions are cross-checked using the standard wave-analysis approach, plus a coordinate trick that makes the wave behavior easier to see.

title: Periodic Analogs of Multiple Black Holes Solutions
abstract: In this article, we extend the numerical studies developed in [arXiv:2210.12898] to construct periodic stationary axisymmetric solutions containing multiple horizons in each fundamental domain. As a direct application, we consider periodic stationary axisymmetric solutions with two identical equidistant counter-rotating horizons. These solutions can be parametrized by the period $L$, the mass $M$, and the absolute value of the angular momentum $|J| >0$. We provide strong numerical evidence for the existence of such configurations, without any restriction in terms of the distance between horizons. This is in sharp contrast with the non-zero total angular momentum case, as it was recently established in \cite{Peraza:2024uto} that static single-horizon periodic solutions cannot be put into rotation if $L < 4M$. It is shown that these solutions do not have any struts on the axis, and it is also explicitly shown that, by taking non-equidistant horizons, struts develop between the black holes. Other global properties of the solutions are also presented.
gpt_response:
Imagine a “pearl necklace” of black holes: identical holes lined up along one axis, repeating forever because space is periodic. Physicists want to know whether such multi–black-hole systems can sit in balance without needing an unphysical “strut” (a defect in spacetime) to hold them apart—a common problem for ordinary two–black-hole setups.

This paper explores a rotating version of that necklace. The authors focus on a repeating pair of black holes that spin in opposite directions, so the *total* spin cancels out. That cancellation matters: far away, the spacetime behaves like a non-rotating, stretched “Kasner-like” universe rather than a rotating “Lewis-like” one, removing a major obstacle that appears when the total spin is nonzero.

To find these solutions, they build an initial guess from known single rotating black holes, then let a computer “relax” it using a heat-flow–style evolution until it settles into a steady state. They confirm the solutions using strict checks (including a mass–area–spin consistency test).

Key results: unlike earlier work, they do **not** see a required minimum separation for existence in this counter-rotating case. But when the holes get extremely close, the numerics become unstable and each horizon’s spin rate seems to blow up—hinting at a real physical limit.

title: Measurements of the production of W$^{\pm}$ and Z$^0$ bosons in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV
abstract: Measurements of the production of the W$^{\pm}$ and Z$^0$ bosons at midrapidity in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV with ALICE at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) are presented. The W$^{\pm}$ and Z$^0$ bosons are detected via their (di)electronic decay channels, with the electron reconstruction performed in the midrapidity region ($|y|< 0.6$). The $p_{\rm T}$-integrated and $p_{\rm T}$-differential production cross sections of electrons from W$^{\pm}$ decays in the interval $30 < p_{\rm T} < 60$ GeV/$c$, as well as the $p_{\rm T}$-integrated production cross section of Z$^0$ bosons, are measured. The results are described by perturbative QCD calculations using different sets of parton distribution functions. The production of W$^{\pm}$ bosons and azimuthally correlated associated hadrons is also measured as a function of the charged-particle multiplicity for the first time at the LHC. The former increases approximately linearly with the charged-particle multiplicity, while for the latter, there are hints of a faster-than-linear increase. These observations are compared with theoretical calculations.

When protons smash together at the Large Hadron Collider, they sometimes create a tiny “fireball” of particles. In big ion collisions this can form quark–gluon plasma, but in small systems like proton–proton collisions the picture is murkier: some patterns look fluid-like, yet there’s little sign of the strong “jet quenching” seen in true plasma.

To sort out what’s really happening, ALICE used a clean probe: W and Z bosons. These heavy particles are born very early in the collision and barely feel the strong force, so they act like impartial witnesses. Using 13 TeV proton–proton data from 2016–2018, ALICE identified W bosons through single high‑energy electrons and Z bosons through electron–positron pairs, carefully subtracting backgrounds from ordinary hadrons and heavy‑flavour decays.

The measured W and Z production rates matched state‑of‑the‑art theory calculations, helping test our knowledge of the proton’s inner quark makeup. Then ALICE checked how production changes in “busy” events: W yields rose roughly linearly with particle multiplicity, but hadrons produced opposite the W increased faster than linear—consistent with simulations including multiple parton interactions and colour reconnection, and hinting that simple counting can be biased by built‑in correlations.

title: Measurement of the charged-particle-jet transverse-momentum fraction carried by prompt and non-prompt J/$ψ$ mesons in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV
abstract: The measurement of the transverse-momentum fraction ($z^{\rm ch}$) carried by prompt and non-prompt J/$\psi$ in charged-particle jets in proton--proton collisions with a center-of-mass energy $\sqrt{s}= 13$ TeV is reported by the ALICE Collaboration at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. The measurement is based on a Transition Radiation Detector triggered data sample corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $\mathcal{L} = 1.63\pm0.03$ pb$^{-1}$. Inclusive J/$\psi$ mesons with transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) above 1 GeV/$c$ are reconstructed at midrapidity through the electron--positron decay channel. The prompt and non-prompt J/$\psi$ contributions are separated using the secondary vertices from beauty-hadron decays. Jets are reconstructed from J/$\psi$-meson candidates and charged particles using the anti-$k_{\rm T}$ algorithm with jet resolution parameter $R = 0.4$ in the pseudorapidity range $|\eta_{\text{jet}}| < 0.5$. The distribution of the charged-particle jet $p_{\rm T}$ fraction carried by the prompt and non-prompt J/$\psi$ mesons, $z^{\rm ch}$, is measured in the range $0.3 < z^{\rm ch} \leq 1.0$ for the jet-$ p_{\rm T}$ range $7 < p_{\rm T}^{\rm jet} < 15$ GeV/$c$. The measured $z^{\rm ch}$ distributions for prompt and non-prompt J/$\psi$ are compared to pQCD calculations and PYTHIA 8 simulations. Prompt and non-prompt J/$\psi$ production within charged-particle jets are found to be qualitatively well reproduced by PYTHIA 8 for $z^{\rm ch}<0.9$, however, as $z^{\rm ch}$ approaches one, the simulations overshoot the measured data, indicating an overestimation of the fraction of isolated J/$\psi$. This observed tension between data and simulations in the highest $z^{\rm ch}$ bins reflects the challenge of simulating hadronization of low-momentum jets.
gpt_response:
When protons collide at the Large Hadron Collider, they can create a short‑lived particle called the **J/ψ**, made of a charm quark and its antimatter partner. Physicists can calculate how the quarks are produced, but **how they “lock together” into a J/ψ** is still hard to predict—especially at low momentum—so it’s a great stress test for particle‑physics models.

ALICE tackled this by looking at **J/ψ particles inside jets**, the narrow sprays of particles produced when quarks and gluons break apart. Using 13‑TeV proton–proton data triggered by a detector specialized for spotting electrons, the team reconstructed J/ψ particles from their **electron–positron decays** and separated **prompt J/ψ** (made directly) from **non‑prompt J/ψ** (from decays of beauty hadrons) by measuring how far the decay happened from the collision point. They then measured how much of the jet’s sideways momentum the J/ψ carries.

Result: in low‑energy jets, **prompt J/ψ often takes almost all the jet momentum**, forming an “isolated” peak. Popular simulations (PYTHIA) match the trend up to high fractions but **overpredict the isolated peak**, highlighting how tricky hadron formation is in this regime.

title: Inclusive $ψ(2S)$ production at midrapidity in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV
abstract: Inclusive production of $\psi(2S)$ mesons is measured for the first time at midrapidity ($|y| < 0.9$) in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV using the ALICE detector at the LHC. The measurement is performed in the transverse-momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) range of 4 to 16 GeV/$c$ and is based on events triggered by the Transition Radiation Detector, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $1.7 \pm 1.8\%$ (syst.) pb$^{-1}$. The $p_{\rm T}$-differential production cross section of the $\psi(2S)$ and its ratio to the J/$\psi$ production cross section are presented. The results extend the accessible $p_{\rm T}$ range down to 4 GeV/$c$, and a mild rise of the $\psi(2S)$-to-J/$\psi$ cross section ratio with increasing $p_{\rm T}$ is observed. The measurements are compared with theoretical predictions based on NRQCD and the ICEM model.

Inside the LHC, protons collide so violently that they can briefly create “charmonium” particles—tight bound pairs of a charm quark and its antiquark. Two famous examples are the J/ψ and its excited cousin, the ψ(2S). ALICE has now measured how often ψ(2S) is produced in proton–proton collisions at 13 TeV, and how that rate compares with J/ψ, focusing on particles flying sideways from the collision point (midrapidity).

To catch these rare signals, ALICE used a special trigger in its Transition Radiation Detector that preferentially records events containing energetic electrons. The team reconstructed ψ(2S) and J/ψ by pairing up electrons and positrons from their decays, carefully subtracting random background combinations using “mixed” events, and correcting the results with detailed computer simulations of the detector.

The new data extend measurements down to lower sideways momentum (4 GeV/c), where other experiments had limited reach. ALICE sees the ψ(2S)-to-J/ψ production ratio rise slightly with momentum. Predictions based on NRQCD match the data well, while the ICEM model tends to give a flatter ratio.

title: Bottom-charmed meson states in inverse problem of QCD
abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of the bottom-charmed ($B_c$) meson spectrum within the inverse matrix QCD sum rules formalism. In this framework, conventional QCD sum rules are recast as an inverse problem, allowing for the direct reconstruction of hadronic spectral densities from first principles without invoking phenomenological continuum parametrizations or quark-hadron duality assumptions. We compute the masses and decay constants of conventional $B_c$ mesons with quantum numbers $J^P = 0^-$, $1^-$, $0^+$, and $1^+$. The obtained results are in close agreement with available experimental measurements and are consistent with predictions from various theoretical and phenomenological approaches. The inverse matrix formulation exhibits improved numerical stability and reduced systematic uncertainties relative to standard implementations, highlighting its suitability for precision spectroscopy of heavy quarkonium systems.
gpt_response:
Inside the particle zoo, the **B₍c₎ meson** is a rare “mixed couple”: one bottom quark bound to one charm antiquark. Unlike charmonium or bottomonium (made from matching pairs), B₍c₎ can’t simply annihilate into light flashes of photons or gluons, so it becomes a clean lab for testing how the strong force builds matter.

This study tackles a long-standing problem: predicting B₍c₎ masses and how strongly these particles “connect” to certain decays (their **decay constants**) without relying on shaky modeling tricks. The authors use an upgraded version of **QCD sum rules**, but flipped into an **inverse problem**: instead of guessing the messy background of higher-energy states, they mathematically **reconstruct the full spectral fingerprint** directly from QCD’s underlying quark-and-gluon calculations.

They compute four main B₍c₎ types (pseudoscalar, vector, scalar, axialvector) and extract their masses and decay constants from peaks in the reconstructed spectrum. The results closely match existing measurements (especially the ground-state B₍c₎ mass) and agree with other theories, while showing improved numerical stability and smaller systematic uncertainties—promising for precision “spectroscopy” of heavy quark systems.

title: Isospin symmetry breaking and the mass of the QCD axion in a three-flavor linear sigma model
abstract: The topology of the ground state of QCD manifests itself through the dependence of its potential energy density on the CP-violating angle $\Theta$. This is computed in the present note within a three-flavor linear meson model. It is shown that the isospin symmetry breaking condensate leads to a 5\% shift in the scale of topological fluctuations, due to which a value emerges in close agreement with lattice QCD determinations. Transparent analytical computation makes explicit the physical content of each step significantly correcting the starting crude estimate of topological susceptibility and eventually achieving the quite accurate final result. This clear physical interpretation lends also a certain pedagogical value to the proposed treatment.
gpt_response:
Inside every proton and neutron, the “strong force” field can occasionally twist into knotted patterns. How often these twists happen is measured by a quantity called *topological susceptibility*—and it also helps set the expected mass of the hypothetical axion, a leading dark-matter candidate.

This paper revisits that number using a three-flavor “linear sigma” meson model (a simplified stand-in for QCD that tracks pions, kaons, and the η/η′ mesons). Earlier versions of such models tended to predict a twist scale around 160–180 MeV, higher than modern lattice QCD results near 75–77 MeV.

The authors separate the calculation into clear steps. First, they estimate a tiny isospin-breaking shift in the quark–antiquark condensate (because up and down quarks aren’t identical). They extract it from the charged–neutral kaon mass difference, using parameters previously fixed by a Functional Renormalization Group analysis—without tuning to the η–η′–π⁰ system.

Next, they include mixing among π⁰, η, and η′ and show that this small isospin violation still nudges the susceptibility by about 4–6%, pushing the prediction closer to lattice QCD. Crucially, the result depends on carefully subtracting electromagnetic effects from the kaon mass splitting, which directly impacts axion-mass estimates.

Imagine a particle that’s like a “mixed-flavor hydrogen atom” for the strong force: the **B₍c₎ meson**, made of a bottom quark and a charm antiquark. It’s special because, unlike many quark–antiquark pairs, it **can’t simply annihilate into light particles**, so its decays mainly reveal the weak interaction. Experiments at the LHC have found a few B₍c₎ states, but much of its “family tree” is still missing.

This study tackles that gap using a revamped version of a common theory tool called **QCD sum rules**. Normally, physicists must guess how higher-energy “background” states behave. Here, the authors flip the problem: they treat it like reconstructing a hidden sound from echoes, **directly rebuilding the particle’s spectral fingerprint** from QCD calculations, which improves stability and reduces systematic uncertainty.

They predict **masses and decay strengths** (decay constants) for four B₍c₎ types: **0⁻, 1⁻, 0⁺, and 1⁺**. The results match existing measurements well, reproduce expected patterns like the **vector–pseudoscalar mass splitting**, and provide precise targets for future collider searches of excited B₍c₎ states.

title: Weak dual symmetries of two color QCD phase diagram
abstract: The phase diagram of two color QCD under influence of baryon density ($\mu_B$), isospin ($\mu_I$), chiral ($\mu_5$ and $\nu_5$) imbalances is investigated within the framework NJL model approach. This letter establishes the existence of weak dualities in two color quark matter--symmetries revealed when full thermodynamic potential is projected or restricted to specific condensation channels. These dualities provide a unified understanding of two interesting phenomena in the phase diagram: universal catalysis and chameleon effect of chiral chemical potential.
gpt_response:
Physicists want a “map” of how matter made of quarks changes under extreme heat and pressure—like in heavy-ion collisions or inside neutron stars. But at high density and low temperature, the usual supercomputer method (lattice QCD) runs into a notorious roadblock called the sign problem.  

This paper sidesteps that by studying a close cousin of real QCD: **two-color QCD**, which keeps key features (confinement, broken chiral symmetry) yet *can* be simulated reliably. The authors use an effective theory called the **NJL model** to track which kind of “collective order” dominates: a chiral condensate, a charged pion condensate, or a diquark condensate (a superfluid-like state).  

Their main discovery is a set of **weak dualities**—hidden swap-like symmetries that appear when you focus on one condensate at a time. These symmetries explain two striking behaviors: **“universal catalysis,”** where a chiral imbalance boosts *all* condensates, and a **“chameleon” effect,** where the chiral chemical potential can mimic other imbalances (baryon or isospin), producing the same phases under the right conditions.

title: ACT-Consistent B-L Higgs Inflation in Supergravity
abstract: We consider a renormalizable extension of the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) endowed by an R and a gauged B - L symmetry. The model incorporates chaotic inflation driven by a quartic potential, associated with the Higgs superfields which lead to a spontaneous breaking of U(1)B-L. Consistency with the ACT data is achieved by considering a fractional shift-symmetric Kaehler potential which includes two free parameters (p,N) constrained in the ranges 1.355<p<6.7 and 6x10^-5<N<0.7. An explanation of the mu term of the MSSM is also provided, under the condition that a related parameter in the superpotential is somewhat small. Baryogenesis occurs via non-thermal leptogenesis which is also realized by the inflaton's decay to the lightest and/or next-to-lightest right-handed neutrinos for normal ordered light neutrino masses.
gpt_response:
Imagine upgrading the Standard Model of particle physics with an extra “charge counter” called **B–L** (baryon number minus lepton number). In this paper, researchers build a supersymmetric version of that idea and use it to connect three big mysteries: **cosmic inflation**, **neutrino masses**, and why the Higgs fields need a special mass parameter (the **μ problem**).

Their key trick is to add new Higgs-like fields that both **break the B–L symmetry** and contain the **inflaton**—the field that drove the universe’s early, ultra-fast expansion. A carefully chosen mathematical “landscape” (the Kähler potential) keeps all other fields heavy and stable during inflation, so the inflaton can roll smoothly. Quantum corrections are checked and shown not to spoil the predictions.

The model’s inflation signals match current telescope data (including ACT) and can produce a **detectable level of primordial gravitational waves**. Because B–L breaks during inflation, it also avoids leftover defects like cosmic strings.

After inflation, the inflaton mainly decays into heavy right-handed neutrinos. Their later decays can generate today’s matter–antimatter imbalance (**leptogenesis**) while staying consistent with neutrino experiments and limits from gravitino production.

title: Parity violation in atoms and electron scattering revisited
abstract: Exchange by two neutrinos (as well as by other fermions) generates a long-range parity-violating (PV) potential of the form $\sim G^2/r^5$, with characteristic range $\hbar/(2m_{\nu}c)$. This interaction produces a $-0.8\%$ correction to the effective weak charge of the Cs atom, thereby resolving the $2\sigma$ discrepancy between the Standard Model prediction and the Cs PV measurement, and yielding $\sin^2\theta_W=0.2375(19)$ at $q^2\approx0$ (to be compared with the Standard Model value $\sin^2\theta_W=0.2387$). We derive updated limits on an extra $Z'$ boson and obtain a constraint on isospin-conserving oblique radiative corrections characterized by the Peskin--Takeuchi parameter, $S=-0.32(53)$ at $q^2\approx0$. The corresponding relative correction to the proton weak charge is $3\%$, and a similar correction is expected for the electron weak charge.
gpt_response:
Physicists know that neutrinos can create an extremely weak force between particles when two of them are exchanged. Far away, this force is tiny and basically impossible to measure. But there’s a twist: the part of the force that violates parity (it treats “left” and “right” differently) becomes sharply concentrated at very short distances. That means it can still noticeably affect precision experiments in atoms and low-energy scattering.

This paper calculates how these “two-neutrino exchange” effects, plus similar loop effects involving other lightweight particles (electrons, muons, quarks, etc.), modify the Standard Model’s predicted “weak charge” of nuclei and protons. The authors treat the short-distance interaction as effectively contact-like, then compute how much it shifts parity-violating signals that mix different electron orbitals in atoms.

Main result: for medium and heavy atoms, the weak charge shifts by about −0.8%. That’s bigger than the current experimental uncertainty in cesium, and it helps remove a previous tension between cesium measurements and the Standard Model. For the proton, the correction is about +3%, consistent with existing scattering data but important for upcoming higher-precision experiments. The paper also argues against a competing claim that nuclear size should erase this correction.

title: On BRST Lagrangian description of partially massless bosonic fields
abstract: We present an exhaustive BRST lagrangian description of partially massless bosonic fields in four-dimensional space. The basic fields are formulated in terms of two-component spin-tensors in (A)dS space where the tracelessness conditions are automatically fulfilled. The mass shell of partially massless fields is reformulated in terms of constraints on Fock space vectors including the second-class constraints. A conversion procedure for transforming second-class constraints into first-class ones is developed, allowing one to construct a Hermitian and nilpotent BRST charge in the Fock space under consideration. It is proven that the hermiticity and nilpotency restrict the conditions on the theory parameters, which are fulfilled only in dS space. The hermiticity of the BRST charge is incompatible with AdS space. The gauge invariant Lagrangian is constructed on the basis of the BRST charge, and for spin $s$ and depth $t$ the allowed states in the Lagrangian include only $(s-t)$ Stückelberg fields. Their exclusion leads to gauge transformations of degree $(s-t)$ for the physical fields. The Lagrangian equations of motion exactly reproduce the mass shell conditions. The Lagrangian in terms of conventional spin-tensor fields is also presented.
gpt_response:
Imagine a particle that’s not quite “massless like light,” but not fully massive either. In curved universes such as de Sitter (dS) or anti–de Sitter (AdS) space, theorists call these in-between objects **partially massless higher‑spin fields**. They behave like massive fields, except that at special “tuned” mass values they suddenly gain extra symmetry—like unlocking new moves in a game—which removes some possible motions. So they carry **fewer physical states than a massive particle, but more than a massless one**, labeled by a **spin** and a **depth**.

This paper builds a general recipe to write down a consistent action (a Lagrangian) for any such bosonic field in 4D. The authors use the **BRST method**, a powerful bookkeeping tool for gauge symmetries, and translate the field equations into an operator language (“Fock space”). A key obstacle appears: the constraints don’t fit BRST neatly, so they apply a **conversion trick** by adding extra auxiliary variables (similar in spirit to the Stückelberg idea).

The punchline is striking: demanding the BRST construction be mathematically consistent forces the theory to be **unitary only in de Sitter space**, ruling out AdS. After eliminating all auxiliary fields, the final theory contains exactly the expected helicity states for partially massless particles.

title: CFT derivation of entanglement phase transition in pseudo entropy
abstract: In this paper, we discuss the entanglement phase transition of pseudo entropy in CFTs. We focus on the case where the in-state and the out-state are different boundary states related by boundary condition changing operators. We compute the pseudo entropy with BCFT methods and find a phase transition with respect to the conformal weight of the boundary condition changing operators. For holographic CFTs, we confirm that the CFT results match that evaluated in AdS.

Entanglement entropy is a famous way to measure how strongly two parts of a quantum system are “linked.” This paper studies a newer cousin called **pseudo entropy**, designed for situations where you start in one quantum state, then **post-select** (force the system to end in) a different final state. In general this quantity can even become complex, but in the setups studied here its meaningful, real part can be extracted.

The authors focus on two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) that have a gravity “hologram” description. They build initial and final states from **boundary states**, and make them different by inserting special boundary operators that change the boundary condition. Using the **replica method** (with twist operators) plus a large‑system approximation common in holographic CFTs, they find a striking “pseudo transition” in time evolution:  
- small boundary change → pseudo entropy grows roughly linearly with time,  
- a critical strength → it grows only logarithmically,  
- large boundary change → it stops growing and becomes constant.  

They also test a free Dirac fermion CFT and find **no transition**: changing the boundary condition doesn’t affect the result, suggesting the effect is tied to holographic/chaotic physics.

title: Magnetized BPS lumps in the $CP^1$ model with Maxwell coupling
abstract: We investigate Bogomolnyi-Prasad-Sommerfield (BPS) topological configurations in the $CP^1$ model minimally coupled to a Maxwell gauge field. Starting from the nonlinear $O(3)$ sigma model, we explicitly construct its classical mapping to the $CP^1$ formulation, emphasizing the emergence of a local $U(1)$ gauge symmetry intrinsically linked to the Fubini-Study target-space geometry. Focusing on the static sector, we analyze magnetized BPS lump configurations. By examining the topological boundary conditions, we show that the magnetic flux is quantized and fully determined by the asymptotic behavior of the gauge field. Within the BPS framework, we identify the specific self-interaction potential required for the existence of self-dual configurations. A detailed analysis of the asymptotic behavior, both near the lump core and at spatial infinity, demonstrates that finite-energy solutions necessarily correspond to lump-like BPS configurations in the $CP^1$ target space, with the scalar field vanishing asymptotically. The resulting BPS equations are solved numerically, and the main physical properties of the solutions are presented. We find that these configurations are regular, magnetically localized, and energetically stable, with their internal structure rigidly controlled by the geometry of the $CP^1$ target space. In contrast to Abelian Higgs vortices, the configurations discussed here do not rely on spontaneous symmetry breaking but arise purely from the geometry of the $CP^1$ target space.

Imagine a flat sheet filled with tiny compass needles (spins). The classic O(3) “sigma model” describes how those needles can twist into stable knots called *lumps*, protected not by glue but by topology—like a knot in a rope that can’t be undone without cutting.

This paper upgrades that idea by rewriting the model in an equivalent language called the **CP¹ model**, where the spin direction is built from a two-component complex field. That rewrite naturally reveals a hidden “phase” freedom, which behaves like an emergent **U(1) gauge field** (similar in spirit to electromagnetism). The authors then couple the system to electromagnetic fields with two extra ingredients: a **Chern–Simons term** (which ties electric and magnetic effects together in 2D) and a **nonminimal, magnetic-moment-like coupling**.

Using a circularly symmetric vortex-style setup, they show the **magnetic flux is quantized**—fixed by boundary behavior—even with these added couplings. A key result from Gauss’s law is that the **electric field cannot generally be turned off**, so the lumps become electrically polarized.

They apply the **BPS method** to find special lowest-energy, stable solutions and determine the required potential. Finally, Runge–Kutta numerics confirm smooth, nonsingular **magnetized BPS lumps**: the scalar field rises then returns to zero, the magnetic field forms a localized ring, and the electric field is localized and even changes sign.

title: A Perfectoid Duality Between M-Theory and F-Theory
abstract: We present a non-singular, definition-level formulation of F-theory by replacing the traditional shrinking-fiber limit of M-theory with compactification on a tower-completed circle described using perfectoid geometry and condensed mathematics. This construction provides an intrinsic eleven-dimensional carrier for modular data and admits a canonical tilting and comparison procedure that yields elliptic geometry as an output rather than an auxiliary input. Using this framework, we establish a precise M-theory/Type IIB dictionary in the constant-coupling sector, showing how the physical axio-dilaton is fixed by eleven-dimensional geometric and topological data. The correspondence is tested at the level of the ten-dimensional bosonic effective action, including its topological couplings inherited from eleven dimensions. The tower-completed geometry naturally organizes global sectors in generalized cohomology, with charge data governed by K-theory and exhibiting a canonical prime-power torsion structure. We further show how this framework extends to varying-coupling backgrounds and duality defects, admits a natural adelic completion with prime-independence, and generalizes to higher-rank and U-duality geometries. We also discuss holographic aspects and the anomaly-refined extension of the duality group beyond the bosonic truncation. Together, these results provide a coherent, non-singular foundation for F-theory and its extensions.

But its usual definition relies on a troubling trick: start with M-theory on a tiny two‑torus and then shrink that torus to zero size while somehow keeping its “shape” information. That shrinking step is mathematically singular, so it hides where the famous duality symmetry really comes from.

This paper proposes a cleaner replacement. Instead of shrinking anything, it builds a new compactification object: a “tower-completed” circle made by stacking infinitely many finer and finer covers of an ordinary circle. To make sense of fields on this non-manifold limit, the authors use condensed mathematics (for consistent gluing of global data) and perfectoid geometry (which packages infinite towers and allows a tool called “tilting”). Tilting plus a comparison step produces an elliptic-curve datum—the geometric home of τ—without collapsing dimensions.

In the constant‑τ case, they match M-theory data to Type IIB: the circle size fixes the coupling strength, a 3‑form holonomy fixes the axion, wrapped M2-branes reproduce the protected (p,q) string spectrum, and the reduced supergravity action matches Type IIB including key topological terms. Extensions to varying τ, defects, and full duality are outlined as future work.

title: Limits on the chiral magnetic effect from the event shape engineering and participant-spectator correlation techniques in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV
abstract: The latest experimental studies related to the search for the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV recorded with the ALICE detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) are presented. Charge-dependent two-particle correlations relative to the reaction plane are measured for charged particles in the pseudorapidity range $|\eta| < 0.8$ and the transverse-momentum range $0.2 < p_{\rm T} < 5$ GeV/$c$. Two approaches have been employed: in the first method, the contribution of the background to the measurement is varied using the event shape engineering (ESE), while the second relies on changing the contribution of the potential CME signal by measuring azimuthal correlations relative to the participant plane, where the background contributions are maximized, and spectator plane, where the CME signal contribution is maximized. Both methods yield results consistent with the absence of a CME signal within the measurement uncertainties. The result obtained from correlations relative to different symmetry planes, a technique applied for the first time at LHC energies, gives the possibility to test independently and confirm the upper limits from previous measurements, while the new limit from the ESE analysis offers improved constraint relative to previous attempts.

When lead nuclei crash together at nearly the speed of light in the LHC, they can briefly melt into a “quark–gluon plasma,” a soup similar to the early universe. Some theories predict that, inside this extreme matter, tiny patches might break a basic mirror-like rule of nature (parity). Combined with an enormous but short-lived magnetic field created by “spectator” protons that fly past the collision, this could push positive and negative charges in opposite directions—a proposed signal called the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME).

ALICE searched for this by tracking millions of particles from 235 million Pb–Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV and studying how pairs of particles line up relative to the collision geometry. They used two strategies: “event shape engineering” (sorting collisions by how elliptical their particle flow is) and comparing correlations measured relative to two different reference planes linked to the participants and spectators.

Both methods saw clear charge-dependent patterns—but these patterns closely followed known background effects, especially local charge conservation combined with elliptic flow. ALICE therefore set upper limits: the CME could contribute at most about 6–7% (95% confidence) in mid-central collisions, with a less strict 33% limit from the plane-comparison method. Larger future datasets should sharpen the test.

title: Deuteron coalescence probability in jets in p-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV
abstract: This article presents the first measurement of the (anti)deuteron and antiproton transverse-momentum distributions, the deuteron coalescence parameter, and the ratio between the yields of deuteron and proton in and out of jets in p-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV. Three regions are used to study the jet-correlated production: Toward, Away, and Transverse to the jet axis, which direction is approximated by the leading particle in the event with $p_{\rm T}^{\rm lead} > 5$ GeV/$c$. The jet contribution is obtained from the Toward region by subtracting the underlying event, which dominates the Transverse region. In p-Pb collisions, an enhancement of the coalescence parameter $B_{\rm 2}$ is observed in jets compared to the underlying event. The enhancement is larger than the one observed in a similar analysis already in pp collisions. The results are compared with predictions from PYTHIA 8.314 using the Angantyr model with a deuteron production model based on ordinary nuclear reactions. The model is able to qualitatively reproduce the large enhancement of the coalescence parameter in jets with respect to the out-of-jets one. The results are further compared in detail with similar ones from previous studies for pp collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV.

When protons and lead nuclei smash together at the Large Hadron Collider, they don’t just spray out single particles—they can also create tiny “atomic nuclei,” like deuterons (one proton + one neutron) and their antimatter twins. But how these fragile bundles form is still debated. One idea says particles emerge from a hot, equilibrated “soup.” Another says nuclei are built later, when nearby protons and neutrons happen to fly out close together and “stick.”

ALICE tested this by comparing deuterons and antiprotons produced **inside jets**—narrow particle sprays from energetic quarks and gluons—versus the **underlying event** outside jets. Using 310 million proton–lead collisions at 5.02 TeV, ALICE identified particles with precision tracking plus energy-loss and timing detectors, then statistically subtracted background and corrected with simulations.

The key result: the “sticking” probability is **over 20 times higher in jets** than outside, a stronger effect than in proton–proton collisions. Deuterons are also more common relative to protons in jets. A popular event generator (PYTHIA+Angantyr) captures the trend but may underestimate jet production at low momentum. These measurements help refine models—and even improve predictions for antimatter nuclei searched for in space-based dark-matter experiments.

title: Measurement of $π^0$-hadron correlations relative to the event plane in semicentral Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV
abstract: Per-trigger yields of $\pi^0$-hadron correlations were measured in semicentral Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV in ALICE at the LHC. The reconstructed $\pi^0 \rightarrow \gamma \gamma$, with a transverse momentum of $11 < p_{\rm T}(\pi^0) < 14$ GeV/$c$, is used as the trigger particle to calculate yields of associated charged particles on the near- and away-side. The photons are reconstructed using the ALICE Electromagnetic Calorimeter, and the charged particles are measured in the ALICE central barrel within a pseudorapidity range of $|\eta|<0.8$. The yields are reported relative to the orientation of the $\pi^0$ with the $2^{\rm nd}$-order event plane, and are background subtracted using the reaction plane fit method. The data give an indication of a suppression of the associated charged-particle yields near $p_{\rm T} \approx 2$ GeV/$c$ when comparing out-of-plane to in-plane trigger particles. At associated charged-particle $p_{\rm T} > 3$ GeV/$c$, no significant event-plane dependence is observed within uncertainties. The results are compared with predictions from the JEWEL model, which implements jet energy loss in an expanding medium. JEWEL predicts no significant modification of either the near- or away-side associated yields, independent of whether medium recoils are included. The observed behavior may indicate the presence of additional energy-loss mechanisms beyond those governed by path-length dependence.

When lead nuclei smash together at the Large Hadron Collider, they can briefly melt into an ultra-hot “soup” of free quarks and gluons, called quark–gluon plasma. Fast quarks and gluons created in the first instant shoot out and form jets—sprays of particles—but the plasma can drain their energy. If a jet travels a longer distance through this soup, it should lose more energy.

ALICE tested this idea in semi-central lead–lead collisions at 5.02 TeV by using a high‑energy neutral pion (identified from its two-photon decay in the EMCal detector) as a jet “marker,” then counting charged particles that appear near it and on the opposite side. Because the collision also produces a huge background of unrelated particles, the team used event mixing plus a “reaction plane fit” method to subtract the background flow pattern, and compared jets pointing in-plane versus out-of-plane.

Result: for associated particles above about 2.5 GeV/c, in-plane and out-of-plane yields look the same within uncertainties. But at lower momenta (1.5–2.5 GeV/c), out-of-plane shows extra suppression, hinting at path-length effects. The JEWEL jet-quenching model predicts almost no angle dependence, suggesting additional energy-loss physics may be missing.

title: First measurement of the strong interaction scattering parameters for the $\mathbf{K^-d}$ and $\mathbf{K^+d}$ systems
abstract: Charged kaon--deuteron interactions offer a sensitive probe of the strangeness sector of QCD at low energy, particularly through their scattering parameters. Despite available theoretical predictions, experimental constraints remain absent, particularly for the $\rm K^{-}d$ system. The first measurement of femtoscopic correlation functions for $\rm K^{-}d \oplus K^{+}\overline{d}$ and $\rm K^{+}d \oplus K^{-}\overline{d}$ particle pairs in Pb--Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV recorded by ALICE at the LHC is presented. Correlation functions for both systems are analyzed in three centrality classes and fitted using the Lednický--Lyuboshitz model to extract the source size and strong interaction scattering lengths. The $\rm K^{-}d$ scattering length is found to be $\Re f_0 = -1.44 \pm 0.15\text{ (stat.)}^{+0.10}_{-0.10}$ (syst.) fm and $\Im f_0 = 1.34 \pm 0.33$ (stat.)$^{+0.21}_{-0.15}$ (syst.) fm, while for $\rm K^{+}d$ the value $\Re f_0 = -0.68 \pm 0.16$ (stat.)$^{+0.09}_{-0.09}$ (syst.) fm is obtained. These results provide the first constraints on the $\rm K^{\pm} d$ interaction modeling at low energy, delivering a long-awaited experimental benchmark for testing chiral QCD dynamics.
gpt_response:
Deep inside every proton and neutron, quarks are glued together by the strong force—yet when “strange” particles join the mix, the rules are still fuzzy. That’s why ALICE at CERN set out to measure how kaons (particles containing a strange quark) interact with deuterons (a proton–neutron pair). Until now, the key case—negative kaons with deuterons—had no direct experimental constraints, because low-energy kaon beams and “kaonic atom” X‑ray studies are extremely difficult.

ALICE used a clever workaround in 337 million lead–lead collisions at 5.02 TeV. By tracking kaons and (anti)deuterons and studying how often they emerge with tiny relative speeds, researchers built “femtoscopic” correlation curves—like reading the afterglow pattern of particles born just femtometers apart. They analyzed three collision centralities and fitted the curves with a standard correlation model to extract both the emission-region size (larger in more central collisions) and the kaon–deuteron scattering lengths.

The result: the first experimental benchmarks for both K⁻d and K⁺d interactions, broadly consistent with theory and crucial for pinning down the hard-to-measure kaon–neutron piece of low-energy QCD.

title: Universal and non-universal finite-volume effects in the vicinity of chiral phase transition in (2+1)-flavor QCD
abstract: In this proceeding, we discuss the finite-size scaling analysis of the order parameter related to the chiral phase transition in QCD with two massless quarks. We use data obtained in lattice QCD calculations performed with highly improved staggered quarks (HISQ) for a range of light quark masses, $1/240 \leq m_\ell/m_s \leq 1/27$ for different spatial volumes ($N_\sigma$) on Euclidean lattices with temporal extent $N_\tau=8$, satisfying $3\,N_\tau \leq N_\sigma \leq 10\,N_\tau$. We observe that infinite volume extrapolated data for the order parameter agree reasonably well with the expected $O(2)$ scaling behavior even for physical ratios of the light-to-strange quark mass ratio. We quantify deviations from asymptotic scaling and perform a detailed analysis of the influence of finite-size effects in terms of temperature and quark masses at a fixed lattice cutoff. This is crucial for improving the reliability of the infinite-volume extrapolated estimate of the chiral order parameter and for a more precise determination of chiral phase transition temperature from direct Lattice QCD simulations.
gpt_response:
When matter is heated to trillions of degrees, the “rules” that give quarks their usual behavior can change. This study zooms in on one such change in quantum chromodynamics (QCD): the restoration of chiral symmetry, a key symmetry that is broken in ordinary conditions. Although simulations strongly suggest this restoration happens through a smooth, second‑order transition, how much another effect—the axial anomaly—matters near the transition is still debated.

To get cleaner answers, the researchers run large-scale lattice QCD simulations (a grid-based way to compute QCD) with 2 light quarks plus a strange quark, using the HISQ method. Instead of assuming the transition must match a particular “universality class,” they build an improved thermometer-like indicator of chiral restoration that cancels troublesome short-distance artifacts, then study how it changes with quark mass and with the finite size of the simulated box.

They find the remaining finite-size distortion follows the pattern expected for an O(2)-type transition and can be fitted reliably. To keep size effects below 1% at physical quark masses, the lattice must be very wide (about 6 times wider than its time extent), and even wider for lighter quarks. Using infinite-volume extrapolations, they estimate the transition temperature (for their lattice setup) to be about 144 ± 4 MeV, consistent with earlier results.

title: Nuclear binding, correlations, and the $A$-dependence of the EMC effect
abstract: The measurements of inclusive electron scattering from nuclear targets carried out at the Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility in the mid 2000s have provided valuable novel information on the $A$-dependence of the modifications of nuclear structure functions known as EMC this http URL argue that these data are best described in terms of the scaling variable $\widetilde{y}$, designed to take into account dynamical effects in interacting many-particle systems, and analyse the $A$-dependence of the slope of the inclusive cross section ratios, $R_A = (\sigma_A/A)/(\sigma_2/2)$, providing a measure of the size of the EMC effect in the region where nuclear binding plays a leading role. The results of our study reveal a linear correlation between $dR_A(\widetilde{y})/d\widetilde{y}$ and the average nucleon removal energy $\langle E_A \rangle$. The role of correlation effects in the determination of $\langle E_A \rangle$ is highlighted.
