In the early 1980s, physicists discovered something odd: when high‑energy particles probe the inside of an iron nucleus, the “per‑nucleon” response isn’t the same as for deuterium (a simple proton–neutron pair). This mismatch—called the EMC effect—shows up most clearly in a middle range of the data, where the ratio drops almost linearly and can reach about 0.8 for heavy nuclei. That was surprising, because nuclear binding energies seem tiny compared with the huge energies used in deep‑inelastic scattering.

This paper revisits the puzzle using a different way to label the data, a variable called “y‑tilde,” which has a simple meaning in the nucleus’s rest frame and makes binding effects easier to spot. The authors analyze Jefferson Lab and SLAC measurements for several nuclei and quantify the EMC effect by the slope of the ratio in the linear region.

They then compute each nucleus’s average “nucleon removal energy” using state‑of‑the‑art quantum Monte Carlo nuclear calculations. The key result: the EMC slopes line up almost perfectly with removal energy, suggesting binding (shaped partly by short‑range correlated nucleon pairs) largely drives the EMC effect’s size and its dependence on nuclear mass.

title: Towards a microscopic description of 12C+12C fusion at stellar energies
abstract: I present a fully microscopic description of the 12C+12C fusion reaction at stellar energies. Utilizing the multichannel Resonating Group Method (RGM), my model explicitly includes 12C+12C and alpha+20Ne reaction channels (with excited states). This approach provides a consistent, simultaneous, description of fusion, elastic scattering, and 24Mg spectroscopy. Results for 12C+12C elastic scattering show excellent agreement with experimental data, significantly improving the single-channel approximations. Spectroscopic analysis reveals that 24Mg states and resonances are highly mixed configurations, contradicting the concept of pure "molecular states." The calculated fusion S-factor is consistent with available experimental data and predicts both narrow and broad resonances near the Coulomb barrier. Main resonance widths originate primarily from the alpha+20Ne exit channels. The S-factor exhibits a decrease at low energies, providing a microscopic support for the hypothesis of fusion hindrance. This work is a first step towards a reliable theoretical extrapolation of the 12C+12C reaction to deep stellar burning temperatures. Future works should include the neutron and proton channels to provide a complete description of the 12C+12C fusion.

Deep inside massive stars, two carbon nuclei can collide and fuse—a key step in “carbon burning” that helps build heavier elements. This study tackles the problem with a fully microscopic computer model that starts from the forces between individual protons and neutrons, rather than using adjustable “absorption” tricks common in older approaches. The author treats the reacting nuclei as clusters and, crucially, includes not only carbon+carbon motion but also the main alternative pathway where the system rearranges into an alpha particle plus neon‑20. That makes the calculation huge, involving tens of thousands of building-block wave patterns.

The model reproduces measured carbon‑carbon elastic scattering much better than simpler one‑channel calculations, predicts several fusion resonances linked to magnesium‑24 states, and suggests a low‑energy decline consistent with possible hindrance—though confirming that will require adding proton and neutron channels in future work.

title: Space-time regions of high baryon density and baryon stopping in heavy-ion collisions
abstract: Four-volumes ($V_4=$ spatial-3-volume$\times$lifetime) are calculated within the model of three-fluid dynamics (3FD) and compared with those of the the JET AA Microscopic Transport Model (JAM). The calculations are performed for central Au+Au collisions at energies $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=$ 3 -- 19.6 GeV. These $V_4$ indicate optimal collision-energy ranges for realizing macroscopic high baryon-density matter. It is found that the 3FD four-volumes noticeably exceed those in the JAM, which indicates a stronger baryon stopping in the 3FD model as compared to that JAM. It is argued that this difference in the baryon stopping correlates with stiffness of the EoS implemented in these models. Contrary to JAM, the four-volume, where a baryon density ($n_B$) exceeds three times the normal nuclear density ($n_0$), does not exhibit a maximum as a function of $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$. It decreases monotonically with increasing $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$, remaining at a fairly macroscopic level (i.e. $V_4\geq 5.5^4$ fm$^4$/c). For higher baryon densities, $V_4$ exhibits maxima in its dependence on $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$. The optimal energy range for densities $n_B/n_0>$ 4 is located at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=$ 3.2--8 GeV. Even for $n_B/n_0>$ 6, the four-volume remains quite macroscopic ($V_4\geq 4^4$ fm$^4$/c) at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=$ 4.5--9 GeV contrary to the JAM.

Think of it as measuring how big and how long the “dense-matter bubble” really is.

They simulate central gold–gold collisions using a three-fluid dynamics model, which treats the incoming nuclei as two baryon-rich streams plus a third “fireball” of newly created particles. They test different assumptions about how compressible nuclear matter is (different equations of state), and compare their results with the JAM transport model.

Main findings: the three-fluid model predicts noticeably larger dense-matter space–time regions than JAM, meaning stronger “baryon stopping” (more slowing and piling-up). For densities above three times normal nuclear density, the dense region steadily shrinks as collision energy rises. For even higher densities, the best energies cluster around roughly 3–9 GeV, where the dense matter remains large enough to be experimentally meaningful.

title: Statistical properties of non-flow correlations in pp and heavy-ion collisions at RHIC energies
abstract: In this work, we have studied the two-particle cumulant in pp, d-Au, and Au-Au collisions. The two-particle cumulant was treated as an event-by-event distribution, and its skewness and kurtosis were analyzed. The non-flow correlations, like jets and decays, constantly produced a skewed distribution, regardless of the model used. On the contrary, HYDJET++ produced a smooth Gaussian distribution at higher $\eta$ windows in fixed impact parameter collisions. The skewness increased consistently for higher $\eta$ windows in all non-QGP models like PYTHIA, PHOJET, QGSJET, and DPMJET. The kurtosis of the distribution also increased with $\eta$ windows in non-QGP models. The skewness and kurtosis of the distributions produced by HYDJET++ decreased with $\Delta\eta$ and eventually reached zero at higher $\Delta\eta$.

The catch is that the same kind of two‑particle “togetherness” can be faked by **non‑flow** effects—especially jets and particle decays—without any QGP. This study looks beyond a single averaged number and instead examines the **event‑by‑event distribution** of a common two‑particle correlation measure.

In HYDJET++, fixed‑geometry heavy‑ion events with hydrodynamics give a near‑Gaussian shape, while turning hydro off brings the skewed tail back. The paper proposes using **skewness and kurtosis trends** as a practical cross‑check for non‑flow contamination in small collision systems.

title: The shape of transverse momentum spectra in hybrid hydrodynamic models
abstract:
We study the scaled transverse momentum spectra over a wide parameter space of state-of-the-art hydrodynamic simulation models in order to learn what information can be obtained from the shape of identified-particle spectra -- previously observed to be surprisingly universal across centrality and collision systems in both experimental data and hydrodynamic simulations. We study its sensitivity to each of 17 model parameters in the context of 4 different models for particlization when switching from the hydro description to the kinetic theory afterburner. We find that the strongest sensitivity is to parameters relating to bulk viscosity, free-streaming time, and the $\texttt{T$_\mathrm{R}$ENTo}$ nucleon width parameter $w$. However, we find that the model generally has surprisingly little flexibility in describing the scaled spectrum observable, despite the large number of parameters.
Within this small range of parameter dependence, we further find significant tension in a simultaneous description of momentum-integrated observables. In particular, while the mean transverse momentum prefers a large value of the nucleon width parameter $w$, a small value is required to obtain scaled spectra that are consistent with experimental measurements. We speculate on the origin of these model tensions and possible missing physics in the commonly-used $\texttt{T$_\mathrm{R}$ENTo}$+free streaming+hydro+afterburner simulation model.

When lead nuclei smash together at the Large Hadron Collider, they briefly melt into an ultra-hot “soup” of quarks and gluons. Physicists usually test their computer models of this quark–gluon plasma by checking simple summaries of the particles that fly out—how many are made and their average sideways momentum.

This study asks: are we missing clues hidden in the *full* momentum “fingerprint”? The authors focus on a clever rescaled spectrum that divides out the total particle count and measures each particle’s momentum compared to the event’s average. Experiments (ALICE) show this rescaled curve looks almost universal across different collision systems and centralities—until higher momenta where other processes take over.

Using the JETSCAPE simulation chain (from initial impact geometry, through fluid-like expansion, to a hadron “afterburner”), the team ran a Bayesian analysis with fast machine-learning emulators and a sensitivity test. They found the universal curve depends only weakly on most model settings, but is most affected by four: early free-streaming time, bulk viscosity strength and peak temperature, and the effective nucleon size.

Crucially, today’s best models still struggle to match the curve’s detailed shape, and fitting it creates tension with fits to average-momentum data—hinting at missing physics, especially for low-momentum pions.

title: Discrete turn strategies emerge in information-limited navigation
abstract: Navigation up a sensory gradient is one of the simplest behaviours, and the simplest strategy is run and tumble. But some organisms use other strategies, such as reversing direction or turning by some angle. Here we ask what drives the choice of strategy, which we frame as maximising up-gradient speed using a given amount of sensory information per unit time. We find that, without directional information on which way to turn, behavioural strategies which make sudden turns perform better than gradual steering. We see various transitions where a different strategy becomes optimal, such as a switch from reversing direction to fully re-orienting tumbles as more information becomes available. And, among more complex re-orientation strategies, we show that discrete turn angles are best, and see transitions in how many such angles the optimal strategy employs.
gpt_response:
Many microbes don’t “steer” smoothly like a car. Instead, they switch between a few simple moves—swim straight, suddenly tumble to a new direction, reverse, or make sharp turns. This paper asks: given noisy sensing, which style climbs a chemical “hill” fastest?

The authors build a math-based simulator of a swimmer whose direction is constantly scrambled by random rotational noise. They compare strategies using a single yardstick: how many bits per second of information flow from “which way I’m pointing” to “what action I take.” By tuning this information budget, they map a speed–information trade-off.

The key result: if the sensor can’t tell left from right (no directional sign), smooth steering is always worse than sudden, discrete reorientations. With very little information, the best move is simply reversing direction; with more information, random tumbles win, and right-angle “flicks” can be best in between. Even when any turn angle is allowed, the optimal solution still uses only a small set of specific angles—discreteness emerges naturally from optimizing under limited information. Similar patterns appear in 3D, where lacking directional cues hurts steering even more.

title: Enhanced Interband Optical Nonlinearities from Coupled Quantum Wells
abstract: The recent, rapid advances in nonlinear chipscale nanophotonics in the visible and near-infrared have been largely driven by manipulating the local dielectric environment proximate to decades-old workhorse bulk nonlinear optical materials, rather than increasing the inherent strength of their nonlinear response. While proposed decades ago, we demonstrate the first experimental realization of a new class of designer nonlinear materials that leverage the interband optical transition in asymmetric structures to provide strong second order susceptibility, $\chi^{(2)}$. Using simple AlGaAs/GaAs coupled quantum wells operating in the near-infrared as a prototype, we observed strong second harmonic generation enhancement of 1550 nm to 775 nm over bulk controls. Extracted $\chi^{(2)}$ values were as high as 2750 pm/V, which is $>$7x that of bulk GaAs. Furthermore, measured susceptibilities agreed well with quantum mechanical calculations of $\chi^{(2)}$ using layer profiles extracted from electron microscopy. Growth interruptions were employed to improve interfacial abruptness in response to electron microscopy characterization, resulting in increased $\chi^{(2)}$ toward the simulation predictions for ideal heterointerfaces. More complex layer designs showed predicted $\chi^{(2)}$ up to 7 nm/V. Such materials are anticipated to find myriad applications, including entangled photon generation at telecommunications wavelengths for chipscale quantum information processing.
gpt_response:
Turning infrared light into visible light is a key trick in modern photonics, but today’s chips usually boost this effect by clever device shapes rather than by making the material itself stronger. This study shows a new route: “designer” semiconductor layers whose internal structure amplifies the effect at its source.

The team built stacks of ultra-thin GaAs and AlGaAs layers called **asymmetric coupled quantum wells**—two wells of different thickness separated by a very thin barrier so electrons can “share” between them. Quantum-mechanical simulations guided the layer design to maximize the material’s ability to double light frequency. The samples were grown with molecular beam epitaxy, transferred onto sapphire to avoid background signals, and tested by shining 1550‑nm telecom light and measuring the generated 775‑nm second-harmonic light while rotating and changing polarization.

Compared with bulk GaAs, the quantum-well stacks produced much stronger doubling: effective values reached **2750 pm/V**, over **7× higher** than bulk GaAs, with a clear resonance near 1560 nm that controls didn’t show. Electron microscopy revealed slightly blurred interfaces; updating simulations with the real layer profiles matched the measurements. Pausing growth at interfaces sharpened them and further improved performance. The authors predict even stronger designs, potentially useful for on-chip quantum light sources at telecom wavelengths.

title: The transient behavior of superconducting multi-cell accelerating cavities
abstract: We employ an equivalent-circuit model of a multi-cell cavity to explore its time-dependent behavior in order to understand differences between the multi-cell model and the commonly-used model of a single-cell resonator. Furthermore, we address tolerances that arise from manufacturing imperfections.
gpt_response:
Superconducting radio‑frequency cavities—the “electric pushers” in particle accelerators—are often simulated as one simple resonator. This paper argues that’s too crude for multi‑cell cavities, which are really chains of slightly different resonators that talk to each other.

The authors build a circuit-style model where each cell is its own resonator, neighboring cells are linked by coupling elements, and the first cell is driven by a generator through an input coupler. They first study the steady “standing-wave” patterns (modes) of a five‑cell cavity and compute the mode frequencies numerically. A key result: the main accelerating pattern (the π‑mode, with alternating field direction from cell to cell) is very sensitive to small coupling errors—tiny manufacturing changes can shift the frequency beyond the cavity’s extremely narrow usable range.

Next they extend the model to time‑dependent behavior (how fields build up and decay when power is switched on/off). Simulations show that although several modes briefly ring at turn‑on, they fade quickly; within about a microsecond the π‑mode dominates and the cavity behaves almost like a single resonator—except it fills about five times more slowly because five cells must store energy. They also quantify tolerances for coupling errors, cell detuning, and “quenches” (sudden loss increases), showing when a single bad cell merely reduces performance versus collapsing the whole field.

title: From synthetic turbulence to true solutions: A deep diffusion model for discovering periodic orbits in the Navier-Stokes equations
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has shown remarkable success in synthesizing data that mimic complex real-world systems, but its potential role in the discovery of mathematically meaningful structures in physical models remains underexplored. In this work, we demonstrate how a generative diffusion model can be used to uncover previously unknown solutions of a nonlinear partial differential equation: the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations in a turbulent regime. Trained on data from a direct numerical simulation of turbulence, the model learns to generate time series that resemble physically plausible trajectories. By carefully modifying the temporal structure of the model and enforcing the symmetries of the governing equations, we produce synthetic trajectories that are periodic in time, despite the fact that the training data did not contain periodic trajectories. These synthetic trajectories are then refined into true solutions using an iterative solver, yielding 111 new periodic orbits (POs) with very short periods. Our results reveal a previously unobserved richness in the PO structure of this system and suggest a broader role for generative AI: not as replacements for simulation and existing solvers, but as a complementary tool for navigating the complex solution spaces of nonlinear dynamical systems.
gpt_response:
Turbulence looks like pure randomness, even though the rules behind it (the Navier–Stokes equations) are known exactly. The authors tackle this puzzle by hunting for “repeatable loops” hidden inside chaos—special flow patterns that come back to themselves after a short time, sometimes only after a shift or flip allowed by the system’s symmetries. In theory, these loops act like the basic “alphabet” from which messy turbulent motion is built.

Finding such loops in a high-dimensional fluid simulation is usually like searching for needles in a galaxy. Here, the team borrows a tool from generative AI: a diffusion model (the same family used for image generation). They train it only on video-like snapshots of swirling vorticity from a 2D turbulence simulation, without giving it the equations or telling it what “periodic” means. After training, they tweak the model so it outputs closed, symmetry-respecting loops, then use a powerful GPU-based numerical solver to “snap” these guesses into exact solutions.

Result: 111 previously unknown relative periodic orbits with short periods (under 3 time units), including 40 under 2—new building blocks for understanding turbulence.

title: Butterfly Echo Protocol for Axis-Agnostic Heisenberg-Limited Metrology
abstract: The extreme sensitivity of chaotic systems to external perturbations makes them natural candidates for sensing applications. We propose a single-shot echo-based protocol for estimating small rotations about an unknown axis that leverages random symmetric probe states prepared via chaotic dynamics. In contrast to previous protocols for this axis-agnostic rotation sensing problem that depend on difficult-to-prepare anticoherent states, the random probe states used in our protocol can be prepared via constant-depth chaotic circuits composed of random one-axis twisting pulses. We demonstrate analytically that our protocol achieves Heisenberg scaling relative to an arbitrary rotation axis that need not be a priori known. We also investigate the effects of collective and single-particle dephasing in our protocol using analytical and numerical tools. While the requirements on dephasing rates to maintain Heisenberg sensitivity are strict, they are achievable in near-term experiments, for instance, for magnetometric rotosensing with high-spin lanthanide atoms such as dysprosium-164.
gpt_response:
Chaotic systems are famous for the “butterfly effect”: tiny nudges can snowball into big changes. Physicists are now turning that sensitivity into a new kind of quantum sensor that can detect a very small rotation—even when you don’t know which direction the rotation axis points.

Their idea is a “butterfly echo” experiment with many atoms acting like a single giant compass needle. First, the atoms start neatly aligned. Next, a short sequence of random “twisting” pulses drives the system into a scrambled, highly entangled state—easy to make compared with the fragile, hard-to-build “perfect” states earlier proposals relied on. Then the unknown rotation happens. Finally, the researchers reverse the scrambling, like rewinding a movie. If no rotation occurred, the atoms return to their original alignment; if a rotation did occur, the rewind is imperfect, and the leftover misalignment reveals the rotation angle.

The team shows (with math plus simulations) that this method can reach the best-possible scaling with atom number, but only over a narrow range of angles and only if dephasing noise is kept very low—still realistic for near-term experiments such as magnetometry with dysprosium-164.

title: Analogue many-body gravitating quantum systems with a network of dipolar Bose-Einstein condensates
abstract: Operational probes of the interface between quantum mechanics and general relativity in the Newtonian regime -- via mass-energy equivalence in clocks or spatial superpositions in interferometers -- share a common description in terms of an effective qubit-qubit Ising coupling. Here we generalize both paradigms to interacting $(N+1)$-level effective qudits made of atomic ensembles with particle number, $N$. The many-body enhancement boosts the signal-to-noise and increases the effective interaction rate, facilitating the observation of gravitationally induced entanglement and decoherence, certified by metrological witnesses based on local and collective measurements. Furthermore, we show that quantum effects induced by gravitational interaction can be simulated by trapped bimodal Bose-Einstein condensates with long-range (e.g. dipolar) coupling, providing a programmable analogue platform to explore gravitating quantum dynamics at accessible time and energy scales. Finally, extending the protocol to a sensor network broadens the entanglement-detection window.
gpt_response:
Gravity is famously hard to “quantize” because the clearest effects are expected at absurdly high energies. Two clever thought experiments try a different route: look for low-energy fingerprints of quantum gravity. In the BMV idea, two tiny masses each travel in a split-path interferometer; depending on which path they take, their mutual gravity changes, potentially creating entanglement. In the CGB idea, the masses are quantum “clocks” whose internal energy affects their gravitational pull, linking gravity to limits on time measurements.

This paper scales both ideas up using Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs): clouds containing many atoms that can occupy two modes (two internal states or two locations). The authors show both setups share the same basic gravity-like interaction, with “local” effects inside each cloud and a “nonlocal” coupling between clouds. Crucially, the local part can be tuned away by adjusting atomic collisions, leaving a clean, gravity-style link between the two clouds.

Because each cloud contains many atoms, the signal becomes stronger—roughly improving with atom number—making entanglement and gravity-induced dephasing easier to spot. Even better, similar interactions can be simulated today using long-range dipolar forces, and small networks of multiple clouds boost sensitivity further.

title: Excited-state quantum phase transitions and chaos in a three-level Lipkin model
abstract: Excited-state quantum phase transitions (ESQPTs) have been extensively studied in two-level models, but their characterization remains challenging in systems displaying mixed regular and chaotic dynamics. In this work, we investigate ESQPTs within the three-level Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model, where an enlarged Hilbert space and multiple separatrices give rise to rich spectral structures strongly influenced by chaos. To investigate the different dynamical regions, we have calculated Poincaré sections and Peres lattices. In addition, by combining chaos-sensitive measures with standard ESQPT diagnostics, we provide a static analysis of ESQPT signatures in this model and establish a robust framework for future studies of its dynamical behavior. The degree of chaos and the Kullback-Leibler divergence are found to be very effective chaos-sensitive measures, which are complementary to ESQPT diagnostics such as the mean field limit and the participation ratio. Hence we provide a standard framework to work with ESQPTs in chaotic three-level systems.
gpt_response:
When water freezes, its properties change suddenly. Quantum systems can do something similar: as you tune a knob in the system, its behavior can “flip” at special points called quantum phase transitions. This paper explores not only changes in the lowest-energy state, but also sharp reorganizations that happen at certain excited energies—so-called excited-state quantum phase transitions.

The authors study a model of many identical particles that can occupy three energy levels (a step up in complexity from the usual two-level case). Adding the third level makes the energy spectrum crowded and messy, with regions that behave regularly and others that look chaotic, which can hide the transition signals.

To untangle this, they combine two approaches: (1) large-scale computer calculations of the energy levels for up to 100 particles, and (2) a “mean-field” approximation that becomes accurate for huge particle numbers and predicts special boundary lines in the spectrum. These boundaries help divide the spectrum into quasi-regular, chaotic, and in-between zones. The team then checks this map using several chaos and transition indicators, finding the clearest agreement when the interaction strength is close to its maximum.

title: Geometric control of maximal entanglement via bound states in the continuum
abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BiCs) convert dissipative open systems into effectively closed quantum subspaces through destructive interference. We show that two identical giant atoms coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide support BICs that coincide with maximally entangled atomic states. Most importantly, entanglement is predominantly determined by the geometric design; the ratio of intra-atomic connection lengths fixes the concurrence, while the propagation phase between atoms selects a family of Bell-like states. We further analyze the dynamical stability of these maximally entangled BICs under exact time evolution, revealing a clear hierarchy of robustness against parameter perturbations. Our results establish an analytical bridge between symmetry, geometry, entanglement, and BICs in giant-atom waveguide platforms.
gpt_response:
Imagine trying to shout into a hallway, but the echoes cancel your voice so perfectly that no sound escapes. Physicists call the quantum version of this a “bound state in the continuum” (BIC): a trapped, long-lived state that sits inside a range of energies where it *should* leak away, but doesn’t—thanks to destructive interference.

This paper explores BICs using “giant atoms”: artificial atoms (often made in superconducting circuits) that connect to a one‑dimensional waveguide at two separated points instead of just one. Those multiple connection points act like built‑in interferometers, letting geometry control how strongly the atoms radiate.

The authors study two such giant atoms coupled to a resonator waveguide in a braided layout. They show analytically that when interference cancels emission, the remaining trapped state is automatically an entangled two‑atom state. Even better, the *amount* of entanglement is set by a simple geometric knob: the ratio of the atoms’ internal connection lengths. Another geometric phase—set by the distance between atoms—selects which Bell‑like entangled state you get.

Finally, exact time‑evolution calculations reveal robustness: small errors in the length ratio hurt entanglement most, while phase or resonance shifts are less damaging. This offers a geometry‑protected route to stable entanglement for quantum technologies.

title: Cryptographic Fragility of Standard Quantum Repeater Protocols
abstract: The security of the proposed quantum Internet relies on repeater protocols designed under the assumption of stochastic, characterizable noise. We demonstrate that in adversarial environments this assumption induces performance vulnerabilities for computationally bounded repeater nodes. We show that the standard BBPSSW distillation protocol recursively purifies error syndromes rather than entanglement. This leads to a state of low fidelity despite diagnostic metrics indicating perfect convergence. Moreover, we show that the verifier cannot check the adversarial influence via the maximum likelihood estimation algorithm since it is blind to computationally bounded observers. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose a Cryptographic Network Stack centered on a trapdoor verification protocol. The protocol exploits private randomness to restore operational stability without requiring channel characterization.
gpt_response:
A future “quantum internet” would send entanglement—pairs of particles linked in a special way—across continents. To do that, quantum repeaters use two workhorse tools: **entanglement purification** (keep the best pairs, throw away the rest) and **tomography** (measure many copies to estimate what noise is present). Most designs assume the noise is random and easy to model.

This paper asks: what if the noise is **deliberately structured**, like an attacker “jamming” the channel, and the repeaters are limited to realistic, efficient (polynomial-time) computations? The authors show a nasty trick: an adversary can inject **pseudoentangled states** that look maximally entangled to any efficient test, even though they contain little usable entanglement. Under this attack, the famous BBPSSW purification protocol can report repeated “success” while the shared state quietly drifts toward an unentangled, useless state. Standard tomography based on maximum-likelihood estimation also becomes effectively blind.

To fix this, the authors propose a **cryptographic network stack**: a “trapdoor” verification using secret random measurement choices, plus a symmetry-based filter (Schur sampling) that rejects the jammer’s states with extremely small acceptance probability.

title: The Magnetic Filling in MAD Simulations and its Impact on the Jet in M87
abstract: Magnetically arrested accretion disks (MADs) in black hole jet launching simulations are very successful in modelling low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (AGN) like M87*. The Fishbone-Moncrief torus is well established for this purpose in numerical astrophysics. The extent of the magnetic vector potential inside the torus that we coin the filling factor has not been studied before in the case of MAD simulations. We employ five 3D general relativistic magneto-hydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations initialized with large-scale tori, that are immersed in weak, poloidal magnetic fields. To study the impact of the spatial extent of the initial magnetic field, hence the magnetic energy content in the torus, we scale it with the filling factor w.r.t. the poloidal geometric area of the mass density distribution. A common choice of the filling factor is complimented and investigated in terms of altered energetics and angular momentum transport. Further, we investigate the polarized, radiative imprints of synchrotron emission on M87 at 86 GHz, comparing them with VLBI observations. Our simulations show that elevated filling factors significantly increase the electromagnetic energy contributions and outward angular momentum transport in the jet, due to the initially increased magnetic energy-content in the torus. High magnetic fillings exhibit increased linear polarization fractions, agreeing with the observed 15% in M87*. We find the jet morphology more prone to disk-vertical flux tubes generated by MAD events. We show, that GRMHD simulations bracket the jet width measurements at the jet base in M87*. Increased magnetic filling of the torus produces jets that are noticeably brighter downstream compared to our reference models, hence, we find high fillings well suited for extended GRMHD jet models of other low-luminosity AGN, as well.
gpt_response:
Messier 87, a giant galaxy 55 million light‑years away, shoots out a famous jet powered by its central supermassive black hole, M87*. To understand how that jet is launched and shaped, researchers ran five high‑resolution 3D computer simulations of gas spiraling into a rapidly spinning black hole. The key twist: every simulation started with the same donut‑shaped gas disk, but the team changed how much of that disk was “filled” with an initial magnetic field.

They checked that the simulations could capture the main turbulence that helps gas fall inward, then measured how much energy the jet carried—separating energy stored in magnetic fields from energy in moving matter. When the initial magnetic field occupied more of the disk, the jet became much more magnetically powered near its base and converted up to about 60% more of the infalling mass energy into outgoing jet power. Stronger magnetic setups also pushed angular momentum outward more efficiently, helping the jet and wind steal spin from the black hole.

Finally, the team created synthetic radio images at 86 GHz, including polarization, and compared jet width and polarization levels with real observations. Some models matched M87’s jet shape well and reached polarization fractions around 15%, similar to what the Event Horizon Telescope sees.

title: Spatiotemporal Thermal Modulation and Patterning using a Programmable 1024 Element Microheater Array
abstract: Programmable microheater arrays are essential for a variety of applications including gas sensing, microfluidic lab on a chip devices, 3D printers, and biosensors that rely on DNA amplification. Increasing the density and number of heating elements directly correlates with the precision with which spatiotemporal heat profiles can be delivered. However, large arrays have thus far not been realized. One challenge is that as the number of elements in an array increases, the complexity of connecting them grows. Here, we show that row-column addressing provides a promising architecture for the efficient operation of a large micro-heater array. We introduce a programmable 32 x 32 microheater array consisting of individually addressable robust platinum (Pt)-based Joule heating elements- each smaller than 300 micrometer. We show that combining high-voltage multiplexed electronics and sequential addressing controlled by a high frequency clock, allows the independent operation of the 1024 microheater elements. We demonstrate the generation of heat images and the patterning of metallic structures formed from the liquid metal Gallium. Our work demonstrates new capabilities for on-chip thermal devices, and opens the possibility to realize novel heat-controlled microactuation systems.
gpt_response:
Imagine a “heat screen” where each pixel can warm up on command. Researchers built one of the largest microheater arrays yet: 1,024 tiny heaters arranged in a 32×32 grid on a silicon wafer. Each heater is a microscopic platinum double-spiral designed to heat efficiently while keeping warmth tightly localized, so nearby pixels don’t blur together.

The big challenge isn’t making one heater—it’s controlling thousands without an impossible tangle of wires. Instead of connecting every pixel separately, the team used a row-and-column addressing system, like how LED displays are scanned. A custom electronics board rapidly selects one row and one column at a time, sending short voltage pulses. By changing how long each pulse stays “on,” they can tune each pixel’s temperature. Infrared camera tests showed clear, sharp patterns (including a smiley face) with at least a 15°C contrast between heated and unheated areas.

To prove this isn’t just a lab trick, they used the array to “thermal print” shapes in gallium metal. Gallium melts just above room temperature, so selectively heating pixels melted chosen regions, letting them remove liquid metal and leave solid letters behind.

title: Coupling–energy driven pumping through quantum dots: the role of coherences
abstract: We study the impact of off–resonant tunneling and coherences on the electron pumping through quantum dots. Thereby, we focus on two electron–pump setups where lowest–order tunneling processes are suppressed and the pump is exclusively driven by modulations of the coupling energy. The first setup is driven by switching on and off the couplings between the quantum dot and the leads, while the second setup employs measurements of the dot occupation. We derive exact solutions for arbitrarily strong tunnel couplings in the absence of Coulomb interaction, identify parameter regimes with optimal pumping currents or optimal energy efficiency, and discuss similarities between both pumping mechanisms.
gpt_response:
Future quantum gadgets will be built from parts so tiny that the usual “classical” rules fail. This paper asks a practical question: when a nanoscale device is strongly connected to its surroundings, can that connection itself be used as a power source?

The authors study a simple setup: a quantum dot (an “artificial atom”) between two electron reservoirs with a voltage difference. The dot’s energy level is kept too high for ordinary, resonant electrons to pass through, so transport can only happen through rarer, off-resonant processes that depend on the dot–reservoir coupling.

They propose two pumping methods that push electrons *against* the voltage by repeatedly destroying quantum “togetherness” (coherence) between the dot and the reservoirs—an action that can inject energy. In scheme 1, the coupling to the left and right reservoirs is switched on and off in alternating steps. In scheme 2, the couplings stay on, but repeated measurements (or a weak continuous detector like a single-electron transistor) erase coherence, similar to the anti-Zeno effect.

Using an exact calculation technique that handles strong coupling and memory effects, they find that structured reservoirs and non-Markovian “echoes” can boost current and even raise efficiency beyond the slow-switching limit.

title: Probing Neutron Skins with KDAR Neutrinos: From Coherent to Diffractive Elastic Neutrino--Nucleus Scattering
abstract: We investigate coherent elastic neutrino--nucleus scattering (CEvNS) induced by pion--decay--at--rest (πDAR) and kaon--decay--at--rest (KDAR) neutrinos, with emphasis on the transition from strict coherence to the diffractive regime. Organizing CEvNS observables in terms of the dimensionless variable qR, we show that πDAR measurements remain confined to the near--coherent region for all nuclei, whereas KDAR neutrinos (Eν = 236--MeV) extend the kinematics into qR ≳ 1, where recoil spectra develop genuine shape sensitivity to the nuclear weak form factor. Using representative light, medium--mass, and heavy nuclei (¹²C, ⁴⁰Ca, ⁴⁸Ca, and ²⁰⁸Pb), we examine relevant cross sections and quantify the statistical sensitivity to the neutron skin thickness achievable at a JSNS²--like facility. For a total exposure of 10--ton·year and realistic KDAR fluences, projected 1σ sensitivities reach ΔRₙₚ⁽⁰⁾ = 0.09±0.02--fm for ⁴⁸Ca and ≈ 0.07±0.02--fm for ²⁰⁸Pb as the fluence increases. These sensitivities are competitive with, and complementary to, parity--violating electron--scattering measurements such as CREX and PREX, while relying on an electroweakly clean neutral--current probe with distinct systematic uncertainties. Our results establish KDAR--based CEvNS as a quantitatively robust and complementary avenue for probing neutron skins and nuclear weak densities beyond the coherent limit.
gpt_response:
Neutrinos are famous for slipping through matter, but every so often one gives a whole atomic nucleus a tiny “kick” and bounces off without breaking it. This rare event—called coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering—gets a big boost when the neutrino’s “view” is too blurry to pick out individual protons and neutrons, so the nucleus responds as one object. Because protons contribute only weakly, the signal mostly tracks where the neutrons are, making it a clean way to study the neutron “skin,” the thin outer layer where neutrons extend beyond protons.

Most past experiments used low-energy neutrinos from stopped pions, which mainly probe the fully coherent, blurry regime—good for counting events, but not very sensitive to the neutron skin’s shape. This paper argues that higher-energy, single-energy neutrinos from stopped kaons can push measurements into a transition region where the nucleus’s internal structure starts to matter, subtly reshaping the recoil-energy spectrum.

Using two standard models of neutron distributions and detailed recoil-to-momentum mapping, the authors project that a JSNS-like setup with 10 ton·years could measure neutron-skin thickness to about 0.03 femtometers in calcium and 0.02 in lead—competitive with leading electron-scattering results.

title: The Universal Eccentricity Distribution for Dynamical Gravitational-Wave Merger Channels
abstract: We argue that all dynamical astrophysical black hole merger channels are expected to result in a common eccentricity distribution at gravitational wave (GW) frequencies relevant for LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA (LVK) in the high eccentricity limit. This follows from the large separation of scales between the GW regime required for creating eccentric mergers in LVK, and the underlying astrophysical formation environment. Our analytical solution shows exceptional agreement with numerical studies. This finding has important implications for both theoretical studies and ongoing searches for eccentric GW sources.
gpt_response:
When LIGO and its partner observatories listen for gravitational waves, they mostly hear pairs of black holes spiraling together in nearly perfect circles. But a few events hint at something messier: “eccentric” orbits, where the black holes swoop past each other on stretched, oval paths. Eccentric mergers are exciting because they usually point to crowded, chaotic environments—like star clusters or triple-star systems—rather than quiet, isolated binaries.

This paper asks a practical question: if a merger is still eccentric when it enters LIGO’s sensitive band (around tens of hertz), what eccentricities should we expect? Many studies assume simple guesswork distributions, but the authors argue that’s not natural.

Their key idea is the “pinhole regime.” To stay eccentric at detectable frequencies, two black holes must pass extremely close on their first encounter—through a tiny “target area” compared with the much larger scales of their birth environment. That makes the final close approach essentially random, wiping out most memory of how the pair formed. Using this scale-separation argument, the authors derive a universal high-eccentricity distribution and confirm it with N-body simulations of binary–single encounters and hierarchical triples. The result provides a better benchmark for future eccentricity searches—and also implies that, at high eccentricity, eccentricity alone can’t reliably tell formation channels apart.

title: Cosmic strings and domain walls: the impact of CMB B-mode data
abstract: We analyse CMB constraints on stable networks of cosmic strings and domain walls using for the first time full Planck 2018 data together with BICEP/Keck 2018 B-mode measurements. The defect-induced anisotropies are computed using the Unconnected Segment Model for Nambu-Goto and Abelian-Higgs strings, as well as for stable domain walls, and included in a full Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis jointly varying all ΛCDM parameters, the tensor-to-scalar ratio, and the string/domain wall tension. No statistically significant evidence for defects is found, although we observe a mild preference for non-zero cosmic string tension. Our results improve previous constraints on the defect power spectrum by up to a factor of two. In the particular case of strings, the improvement is driven by the B-mode data, and is especially pronounced for Abelian-Higgs strings. We also present forecasts for upcoming Simons Observatory data and find that, with the baseline noise configuration, the constraints on the string tension could improve by about a factor of three. Finally, we assess the impact of Nambu-Goto string loops on CMB anisotropies in light of both current and future observations.
gpt_response:
Physicists usually hunt for new laws of nature by smashing particles together, but some “new physics” could be written across the sky. Two candidates are **cosmic strings** (ultra-thin cracks in space) and **domain walls** (sheet-like boundaries), which may have formed when the early Universe cooled and changed phase.

This study updates the search for these relics using the Universe’s oldest light: the **cosmic microwave background (CMB)**. The team combines the latest **Planck 2018** maps with **BICEP/Keck 2018** measurements of the CMB’s special “twist” pattern (B-mode polarization), plus Planck’s lensing data.

Because full simulations are expensive, they use a fast, semi-analytic recipe: model strings and walls as many randomly placed, randomly moving segments or patches, tuned to match known network behavior, then compute the CMB patterns with the CMBACT4 code. They test two string types (Nambu–Goto and Abelian–Higgs) and include string loops.

Result: **no detection**, but tighter limits. String tension must be below about **1.2×10⁻⁷** (Nambu–Goto) or **1.8×10⁻⁷** (Abelian–Higgs), and domain walls below about **0.81 MeV** (in the paper’s units). They also forecast that the **Simons Observatory** could improve string limits by roughly a factor of 2–3, especially thanks to better B-mode data.
